name: Subaru FB25
fullName: Subaru FB25 2.5L DOHC 16-valve horizontally opposed four
summary: The FB25 is a chain-driven boxer whose cams live in separate bolt-on cam carriers, so the valvetrain comes off as two sealed modules and cam clearance is set with shims under roller rockers. Unlike the older EJ engines it has no piston pin service holes: the diagonally split rods let each piston and rod come out through its bore once the heads and oil pan upper are off, and only then is the block split. Almost every joint is sealed with liquid gasket and nearly every major fastener is angle-torqued, so most rebuild mistakes are sealing, sequence and timing-mark errors.

facts.label: Layout
facts.value: Horizontally opposed (boxer) four, DOHC, 4 valves per cylinder

facts.label: Timing drive
facts.value: Two timing chains (RH and LH bank) with hydraulic tensioners

facts.label: Valvetrain
facts.value: Roller rocker arms with selective valve shims; dual AVCS on intake and exhaust

facts.label: Fuel injection
facts.value: Port (multipoint) injection, injectors in the cylinder heads

facts.label: Block material
facts.value: Aluminum, open deck, cast iron liners, split vertically into RH and LH halves

facts.label: Connecting rods
facts.value: Diagonally split; pistons and rods come out through the bores

facts.label: Oil capacity
facts.value: 5.7 L (6.0 US qt) at overhaul, 0W-20 synthetic

facts.label: Coolant capacity
facts.value: About 7.6 L (8.0 US qt), CVT model

notes: Specs here come from the 2014 Forester service manual (FB25, Mechanical ME(H4DO)). Later 2015 to 2018 Forester engines may carry running changes, so check numbers against Subaru STIS for the exact VIN before torquing anything.

There are no piston pin service holes on the FB25. Pistons and rods leave and enter through the bores, with the rod caps reached from the oil pan side, which is why the heads and oil pan upper come off before the block is split.
The engine comes out without the TR580; the torque converter stays in the transmission and needs the converter stopper fitted before the engine is pulled away.

Special tools that matter: crankshaft socket 18252AA000, rod bolt socket 18270AA020, cam sprocket socket 18270KA010, pulley wrench 18355AA000 with pin sets, angle gauge, valve spring compressor, rear seal guide and installer, and the chain cover removal kit J-53038 with alignment pins J-51972.
Treat as one-time use: connecting rod cap bolts, head gaskets, every O-ring, AVCS filter screens, the oil separator cover, valve stem seals, front and rear crank seals, and any replaced valve shim.
Liquid gasket is ThreeBond 1217G per the manual (ThreeBond 1105 on gallery plug threads, 1141G on the PCV valve). Most joints must be assembled within five minutes of applying the bead.
Usually sublet to a machine shop: head and deck surfacing, valve guide replacement and seat cutting, boring and honing (all four bores at once), crank grinding and rod bushing replacement.
Typical rebuild kits omit the oil pump and timing parts. The oil pump is built into the chain cover and is not serviceable separately.

phases.name: Prep and engine removal
phases.summary: Check the engine, drain it, disconnect it and lift it out of the Forester leaving the TR580 in the car.

phases.name: External and timing teardown
phases.summary: Mount on a stand, strip the intake and accessories, open the chain cover and park the valvetrain safely as the chains come off.

phases.name: Cylinder heads and valvetrain
phases.summary: Lift off the cam carriers with their camshafts, remove both heads and strip the valves.

phases.name: Short block teardown
phases.summary: Pull pistons and rods out through the bores, split the block halves and strip the crankshaft and pistons.

phases.name: Cleaning, inspection and measurement
phases.summary: Clean everything and measure the head, valvetrain, bores, pistons, rods and crankshaft against the factory limits.

phases.name: Machine shop decisions
phases.summary: Decide what gets resurfaced, cut, bored, ground or replaced, and order the one-time parts.

phases.name: Short block assembly
phases.summary: Join the block halves around the crankshaft, then fit pistons and rods through the bores and close up the bottom end.

phases.name: Heads and cam carriers
phases.summary: Build and torque the heads, fit the rocker gear and cam carriers, and set cam clearance with shims.

phases.name: Timing chains, AVCS and covers
phases.summary: Time both chains to their colored links, close the rocker and chain covers and fit the crank pulley.

phases.name: External assembly
phases.summary: Refit the intake side, sensors and accessories.

phases.name: Installation, first start and break-in
phases.summary: Install the engine, fill and bleed it, prime the oil system, start it and break it in.

steps.title: Record compression before teardown
steps.action: With the engine warm, disable the fuel pump at its fuse, pull all four plugs, hold the throttle wide open and crank each cylinder on a compression gauge at least twice, then refit the plugs.
steps.why: A baseline reading tells you which cylinders to look at hardest once it is apart; it has to happen while the engine can still run.
tools: Compression gauge (screw-in end under 25 mm long)

spec.note: 152 to 203 psi; no more than 100 kPa (14 psi) between cylinders

mistakes.title: Compression tested under bad conditions
mistakes.what: Running the test cold, with a tired battery, with the throttle closed or with only some plugs out.
mistakes.consequence: Every cylinder reads low, so a genuinely weak cylinder hides among the others and the teardown loses its best clue.
mistakes.prevent: Test warm, on a charged battery, with all four plugs out, the throttle held wide open and the same number of strokes per cylinder.
mistakes.detect: Readings that are all low but even point at the test setup rather than the engine.

mistakes.title: No baseline recorded before removal
mistakes.what: Pulling the engine without writing down compression, oil use, smoke and stored codes.
mistakes.consequence: Once apart, nobody can say which cylinder had the ring, valve or gasket fault, so the cause may be built back in.
mistakes.prevent: Record per-cylinder compression, the oil consumption history and any codes (AVCS, misfire) before the first bolt comes out.

steps.title: Recover A/C refrigerant
steps.action: Have the A/C system evacuated with a recovery machine before any refrigerant line is opened.
steps.why: The compressor leaves with the engine, so its hoses must be disconnected, and refrigerant may not be vented.

mistakes.title: A/C lines opened before recovery
mistakes.what: Disconnecting the compressor hoses while the system still holds refrigerant, or leaving the opened ports uncapped.
mistakes.consequence: Refrigerant vents (illegal and a frostbite hazard) and moist air and dirt enter the system, which the later recharge cannot fully remove.
mistakes.prevent: Have the system recovered first, then cap every opened line and compressor port straight away.

steps.title: Relieve fuel pressure, disconnect battery
steps.action: Bleed fuel pressure using the factory procedure, remove the fuel filler cap to vent the tank, then disconnect the battery ground.
steps.why: Fuel lines are opened later; relieving pressure first keeps fuel from spraying, and the ground comes off before any connector is unplugged.

mistakes.title: Fuel line opened under pressure
mistakes.what: Releasing a fuel quick connector before the pressure has been bled off.
mistakes.consequence: Fuel sprays across a warm engine bay, which is a fire risk and soaks the harness and belts.
mistakes.prevent: Run the factory pressure relief, open the filler cap, and wrap the connector in a shop towel as it is released.

mistakes.title: Connectors pulled with battery live
mistakes.what: Unplugging harness connectors or the generator lead with the battery ground still connected.
mistakes.consequence: A dropped live terminal can short to the block, blowing a fusible link or damaging a control module.
mistakes.prevent: Remove the battery ground cable before any electrical connector, and keep the cable end away from the post.

steps.title: Drain the coolant
steps.action: Fit a hose to the radiator drain, open the drain plug with the radiator cap off and collect the coolant; refit the drain with new O-rings.

mistakes.title: Coolant left trapped in the engine
mistakes.what: Draining with the radiator cap on, or only from the radiator, so the block and heads stay partly full.
mistakes.consequence: Coolant pours out when the heads come off and can run into the bores and crankcase, where it corrodes bearing and journal surfaces.
mistakes.prevent: Open the radiator cap before draining and expect more coolant when the water pipes and heads are removed; keep rags and a pan ready.

mistakes.title: Drain plug O-ring reused
mistakes.what: Refitting the radiator drain plug with its old O-rings.
mistakes.consequence: A slow coolant drip appears after the rebuild, and a low level can cause overheating.
mistakes.prevent: Fit new drain plug O-rings as the procedure calls for.

steps.title: Drain oil and remove filter
steps.action: Open the filler cap, drain the oil from the pan, refit the drain plug with a new gasket and spin off the oil filter.
steps.why: The pan has to be empty before the engine is tipped on the stand and the pan is split.

mistakes.title: Old oil and filter discarded unread
mistakes.what: Draining the oil and throwing the filter away without looking at either.
mistakes.consequence: The evidence of what failed is lost: glitter means bearing wear, milky oil means coolant, and sludge points at the AVCS and PCV problems.
mistakes.prevent: Drain into a clean pan, look at the oil in good light, and cut the filter open before scrapping it.
mistakes.detect: Metal flakes in the filter pleats or a milky film on the dipstick.

mistakes.title: Drain plug threads stripped
mistakes.what: Overtightening the drain plug or reusing a flattened gasket.
mistakes.consequence: The aluminum pan threads strip or the plug weeps oil, and a leaking pan has to come off later.
mistakes.prevent: Use a new drain plug gasket and a torque wrench set to the drain plug value.

steps.title: Remove intake ducting and radiator
steps.action: Take out the air intake duct and boot, the rear air cleaner case and the radiator.
steps.why: The radiator sits directly in front of the crank pulley and must be out of the way for the engine to roll forward.

mistakes.title: Open intake left uncovered
mistakes.what: Leaving the throttle body or manifold opening uncapped once the intake duct and air cleaner are off.
mistakes.consequence: Grit or a loose nut falls into the manifold and is later drawn into a cylinder, scoring the bore or hitting a valve.
mistakes.prevent: Tape or cap every intake opening as soon as it is exposed.

mistakes.title: Radiator core crushed on removal
mistakes.what: Levering the radiator out against the fan shroud or setting it down on its fins.
mistakes.consequence: Bent fins or a cracked tank reduce cooling, and the new engine can run hot during break-in.
mistakes.prevent: Lift the radiator straight up with both hands and store it on edge away from the work area.

steps.title: Label and disconnect engine harness
steps.action: Tag and unplug the bulkhead harness connectors, generator and A/C compressor leads, and the engine ground strap; free the harness from its clips.
steps.why: Labels now save hours at reinstallation when dozens of identical-looking connectors go back.

mistakes.title: Connectors not labeled
mistakes.what: Unplugging the bulkhead and sensor connectors without tagging them.
mistakes.consequence: Look-alike connectors get swapped at reinstallation, giving no-start conditions or confusing sensor codes.
mistakes.prevent: Tag both halves of every connector and photograph the harness routing before unclipping it.

mistakes.title: Connector locks broken
mistakes.what: Pulling connectors by their wires or levering the locking tabs with a screwdriver.
mistakes.consequence: A broken lock lets the connector back off with vibration, causing intermittent faults that are hard to trace.
mistakes.prevent: Press the release fully and pull on the connector body only.

steps.title: Disconnect hoses and fuel lines
steps.action: Disconnect the brake booster hose, heater inlet and outlet hoses, CVTF cooler water hose, A/C pressure hose, and the fuel delivery and evaporation lines using the quick-connector release tool.
steps.mistake: Swapping the heater inlet and outlet hoses at reassembly is easy if they are not marked now.

mistakes.title: Heater hoses not marked
mistakes.what: Disconnecting the heater inlet and outlet hoses without tagging which is which.
mistakes.consequence: They are easy to swap at reinstallation, and swapped hoses give poor heat and trap air in the system.
mistakes.prevent: Tag each hose and its pipe with matching labels before pulling them off.

mistakes.title: CVT fluid cooler lines disturbed
mistakes.what: Disconnecting the short CVT fluid lines at the cooler instead of just the engine coolant hoses.
mistakes.consequence: CVT fluid is lost and dirt can enter the transmission circuit, and the CVTF level then has to be corrected.
mistakes.prevent: Disconnect only the coolant hoses and move the cooler on its bracket, leaving the short CVTF lines undisturbed.

mistakes.title: Quick connector forced off
mistakes.what: Prying fuel and evaporation quick connectors without the release tool.
mistakes.consequence: The connector or its retainer cracks and leaks fuel after restart.
mistakes.prevent: Use the correct release tool and inspect each connector body and retainer before reuse.

steps.title: Remove exhaust and lower bolts
steps.action: From underneath, remove the front exhaust pipe and the lower transmission-to-engine bolts and nuts, then remove the nuts holding the engine mounts to the crossmember.

mistakes.title: Exhaust studs snapped at the head
mistakes.what: Forcing seized front exhaust pipe nuts without soaking or working them.
mistakes.consequence: A stud breaks in the cylinder head and has to be extracted, adding machine work.
mistakes.prevent: Soak the nuts with penetrating oil, work them back and forth, and stop if a stud starts to twist.

mistakes.title: Pipe hung on the sensor harness
mistakes.what: Letting the front exhaust pipe hang by the air-fuel sensor wiring as it drops.
mistakes.consequence: The sensor lead or connector is damaged, giving sensor codes after the rebuild.
mistakes.prevent: Unplug the sensor first and support the pipe while the last fasteners come out.

steps.title: Unbolt converter from drive plate
steps.action: Remove the service hole plug, turn the crank by the pulley bolt to reach each of the torque converter bolts and remove them.
steps.why: On the Forester the engine comes out alone and the TR580 stays in the car, so the converter must be freed from the drive plate first.

mistakes.title: Converter bolt left in
mistakes.what: Losing count and pulling the engine with one torque converter bolt still installed.
mistakes.consequence: The drive plate bends or the converter is dragged forward off its pump drive, damaging the transmission.
mistakes.prevent: Count the bolts out against the total and turn the crank once more to look at every bolt position through the service hole.

steps.title: Support the engine and transmission
steps.action: Hang the engine from a hoist with chains or wire rope and put a jack under the transmission.
steps.why: Once the bellhousing bolts are out, the transmission would otherwise drop on its rear mount.

mistakes.title: Transmission left unsupported
mistakes.what: Removing the bellhousing bolts before a jack is under the transmission.
mistakes.consequence: The transmission drops onto its rear mount, straining the mount, lines and harness.
mistakes.prevent: Set the jack under the transmission before the upper bellhousing bolts come out.

mistakes.title: Transmission jacked too high
mistakes.what: Raising the transmission further than needed to reach the mount hardware.
mistakes.consequence: The transmission is pushed up into the bulkhead and tunnel, which can damage the case, harness or body.
mistakes.prevent: Raise it only enough to remove the mount fasteners, watching the clearance at the bulkhead.

steps.title: Fit converter stopper, separate bellhousing
steps.action: Remove the starter, attach the torque converter stopper to the converter housing, then remove the upper transmission-to-engine bolts.
steps.why: The stopper keeps the converter seated on the transmission input shaft as the engine pulls away.
steps.mistake: Pulling the engine without the stopper lets the converter slide off its shaft and damage the pump drive and seal.

mistakes.title: Engine pulled without converter stopper
mistakes.what: Separating the engine from the TR580 without the torque converter stopper fitted.
mistakes.consequence: The converter slides off the input shaft and damages the pump drive and the converter seal.
mistakes.prevent: Bolt the stopper to the converter housing before the upper bellhousing bolts come out.

mistakes.title: Prying on the bellhousing seam
mistakes.what: Wedging a bar into the machined joint between the engine and the CVT case to break them apart.
mistakes.consequence: The mating faces are gouged or the case is cracked, causing leaks or misalignment when the engine goes back.
mistakes.prevent: Use only the pry relief point near the engine number, apply light pressure, and never twist the tool.

steps.title: Lift the engine out
steps.action: Raise the engine slightly, raise the transmission with the jack, slide the engine forward until it clears the transmission, then lift it out slowly.
steps.why: The engine must move straight forward off the transmission before it can be lifted, or the input shaft and converter take side load.
steps.mistake: Swinging the engine early catches the crank pulley or dipstick on the body and radiator support.

mistakes.title: Engine swung before it is clear
mistakes.what: Tilting or swinging the engine before it has moved far enough forward.
mistakes.consequence: The crank pulley or dipstick catches the body or radiator support and is bent or broken.
mistakes.prevent: Move the engine straight forward first and watch the pulley and dipstick as it comes up.

mistakes.title: Lifting before the shaft clears
mistakes.what: Raising the engine while the converter and input shaft are still engaged with it.
mistakes.consequence: The input shaft or converter pilot takes a side load and the pump or seal is damaged.
mistakes.prevent: Slide the engine straight forward until it is completely clear of the transmission before lifting.

mistakes.title: Engine lifted by the crank nose
mistakes.what: Using the crankshaft snout or a pulley as a lifting or steadying point.
mistakes.consequence: The crank nose, seal bore or chain cover is damaged.
mistakes.prevent: Lift only by the engine hangers, with chains or wire rope rated for the load.

steps.title: Mount the engine on stand
steps.action: Remove the engine mounts and bolt the engine to the stand using the RH and LH stand adapters and the adapter plate.

mistakes.title: Stand bolted to the oil pan studs
mistakes.what: Mounting a generic engine stand to the studs in the oil pan upper instead of the block mounting holes.
mistakes.consequence: The cast pan flexes or cracks under the engine weight, and its seal to the block is disturbed.
mistakes.prevent: Use the factory stand adapters, or the four block mounting holes on a generic stand.

mistakes.title: Stand bolts too short or loose
mistakes.what: Engaging only a few threads in the aluminum, or skipping the adapter bolt torque.
mistakes.consequence: Threads pull out as the engine is rotated and the engine can fall off the stand.
mistakes.prevent: Use bolts with full thread engagement and torque them to the stand adapter spec.

steps.title: Remove the V-belt
steps.action: Turn the belt tensioner clockwise with a wrench to relieve tension and slip the belt off, then remove the tensioner and the idler pulley.
steps.why: Every pulley on the front of the engine, including the crank pulley, is blocked by the belt.

mistakes.title: Belt tensioner allowed to snap back
mistakes.what: Letting the tensioner arm spring back after the belt slips off.
mistakes.consequence: The tensioner damper is damaged or a hand is pinched; a weak tensioner then lets the new belt slip.
mistakes.prevent: Hold the wrench and return the arm slowly to its stop.

mistakes.title: Belt routing not recorded
mistakes.what: Removing the V-belt without noting its path.
mistakes.consequence: The belt goes back wrong and a pulley turns backward or the belt walks off.
mistakes.prevent: Photograph the routing before the belt comes off.

steps.title: Remove generator and A/C compressor
steps.action: Unbolt and remove the generator and the A/C compressor from their brackets.
steps.why: The compressor mounts to the LH head and must come off before that head; the generator blocks the chain cover.

mistakes.title: Compressor ports left open
mistakes.what: Leaving the A/C compressor ports uncapped while it sits on the bench.
mistakes.consequence: Moisture and dirt enter the compressor, shortening its life after the system is recharged.
mistakes.prevent: Cap both ports as soon as the hoses are off and keep the compressor upright.

steps.title: Remove the intake manifold
steps.action: Disconnect the EGR pipe, PCV hose, MAP and throttle connectors and fuel delivery pipes, then lift the manifold off the tumble generator valves and remove the engine wiring harness.

mistakes.title: Manifold lifted with a hose attached
mistakes.what: Lifting the intake manifold while a PCV, vacuum or EGR connection is still made.
mistakes.consequence: An aged plastic hose or fitting cracks, leaving a vacuum leak or a PCV fault after the rebuild.
mistakes.prevent: Check each side of the manifold with a light before lifting and replace any brittle hose found.

steps.title: Remove tumble generator valves
steps.action: Unplug and unbolt the tumble generator valve assemblies from each head, then remove the cylinder head plates behind them.

mistakes.title: TGV sealing face gouged
mistakes.what: Prying the tumble generator valve bodies off the head plates with a screwdriver.
mistakes.consequence: The scratched flange leaks air after assembly, giving lean codes and a rough idle.
mistakes.prevent: Break the joint with a plastic tool and protect the flange faces on the bench.

steps.title: Remove the EGR pipe
steps.action: Unbolt the EGR pipe from the water pipe and the RH block half.
steps.why: It ties the RH head to the block and blocks the RH head from lifting off.

mistakes.title: EGR pipe bent free
mistakes.what: Twisting the EGR pipe off its block and water pipe mounts after a fastener is missed.
mistakes.consequence: The pipe or its flange cracks, causing an exhaust leak or EGR flow codes.
mistakes.prevent: Confirm every EGR fastener is out and lift the pipe straight off.

steps.title: Remove coils and spark plugs
steps.action: Remove the four ignition coils and spark plugs.
steps.why: Pulling the plugs lets the crank turn freely without compression while the timing is set up.

mistakes.title: Spark plugs not read
mistakes.what: Throwing the old plugs away without laying them out by cylinder.
mistakes.consequence: Oil fouling or coolant residue on one plug, which points to a ring, guide or gasket fault there, is lost.
mistakes.prevent: Lay the plugs out in cylinder order and note their condition with the compression readings.

mistakes.title: Debris left in plug wells
mistakes.what: Pulling the plugs without blowing out the plug tubes first.
mistakes.consequence: Grit drops into the cylinder and is dragged along the bore as the crank is turned for timing removal.
mistakes.prevent: Blow out each plug well with compressed air before loosening the plug.

steps.title: Remove water pump pulley
steps.action: Hold the water pump pulley with the pulley wrench and pin set and remove its bolts.

mistakes.title: Pump pulley held with pliers
mistakes.what: Gripping the water pump pulley grooves with pliers instead of the pulley wrench.
mistakes.consequence: The pulley groove is burred and wears the new belt.
mistakes.prevent: Hold the pulley with the pulley wrench and pin set.

steps.title: Loosen and remove crank pulley
steps.action: Lock the crank pulley with the pulley wrench and pin set, break the bolt loose and remove the bolt and pulley.
steps.why: The crank must be held by the pulley itself; the bolt is angle-torqued and will not break loose otherwise.

mistakes.title: Crank locked through the ring gear
mistakes.what: Jamming a screwdriver into the drive plate teeth to stop the crank turning.
mistakes.consequence: Ring gear teeth break or the drive plate bends, which shows up later as starter grinding.
mistakes.prevent: Lock the crank pulley with the pulley wrench and pin set, as the procedure specifies.

mistakes.title: Pulley knock pin lost
mistakes.what: Letting the pulley locating pin fall out unnoticed when the pulley comes off.
mistakes.consequence: Without its pin the pulley cannot be indexed to the crank at reassembly and the job stalls.
mistakes.prevent: Check the pin is in place and bag it with the pulley bolt.

steps.title: Strip harness from chain cover
steps.action: Unplug the oil control solenoids, cam position sensors, oil pressure switch, oil temperature sensor and oil level switch, remove the harness stay, and pull the dipstick guide and idler pulley.

mistakes.title: Sensor connectors cracked
mistakes.what: Forcing the brittle oil control solenoid and cam sensor connectors off the chain cover.
mistakes.consequence: A damaged connector gives intermittent AVCS or cam position codes after the rebuild.
mistakes.prevent: Release each lock fully and support the sensor body while unplugging.
mistakes.detect: The AVCS bulletin checks connector pins and circuit resistance first when these codes appear.

steps.title: Separate the chain cover
steps.action: Remove all chain cover bolts and push the cover off with the factory removal tool, or pry only at the designated points with a taped bar, working around a little at a time.
steps.why: The cover is sealed with a long bead of liquid gasket to both heads, both cam carriers, the block and the oil pan upper; it has to come off before any timing part is reachable.
steps.mistake: Prying on the unsupported lower corner of a cam carrier cracks the cam cap and scraps the whole carrier.

mistakes.title: Pried on cam carrier lower corner
mistakes.what: Levering against the unsupported lower corner of a cam carrier to free the cover.
mistakes.consequence: The cam cap cracks, and a cracked cap means replacing the whole cam carrier.
mistakes.prevent: Pry only at the designated points, never on the lower carrier corner.

mistakes.title: Metal or power tools on the seam
mistakes.what: Driving a steel pry bar, chisel or air tool into the joint to break the sealant.
mistakes.consequence: The machined aluminum faces are scratched, leaving a permanent leak path that can mean a new cover or carrier.
mistakes.prevent: Use the push-off kit with hand tools only and a plastic trim tool once a gap opens.

mistakes.title: A cover bolt left in
mistakes.what: Starting to push or pry the cover with one of its many bolts still fitted.
mistakes.consequence: The cover ear or boss cracks, and the cover (with the oil pump built in) has to be replaced.
mistakes.prevent: Count the bolts out and check every hole with a light before applying any force.

mistakes.title: Removal bolts turned unevenly
mistakes.what: Running one push-off bolt in far ahead of the others.
mistakes.consequence: The cover cocks on its dowels and binds or cracks instead of lifting evenly.
mistakes.prevent: Turn the removal bolts half a turn at a time, alternating left to right and upper to lower.

mistakes.title: Cover stored face up as a tray
mistakes.what: Setting the removed chain cover sealing face up and piling parts in it.
mistakes.consequence: The machined sealing face is nicked and leaks after reassembly.
mistakes.prevent: Store the cover front face down on a clean towel and keep other parts out of it.

steps.title: Clean off cover sealant
steps.action: Remove the O-rings at the heads, block LH and oil pan upper and strip the old liquid gasket from the cover and engine with gasket remover and plastic scrapers.
steps.why: Steel blades and abrasive discs gouge the machined aluminum faces and cause leaks later.

mistakes.title: Steel scraper or abrasive disc used
mistakes.what: Cleaning the old sealant off with a steel razor blade, wire wheel or abrasive disc.
mistakes.consequence: The aluminum faces are gouged and the abrasive grit gets into the oil passages.
mistakes.prevent: Soak with gasket remover and use white plastic razor blades or a sharpened plastic trim stick.

mistakes.title: Sealant flakes into oil passages
mistakes.what: Scraping sealant with the oil holes in the cover, carriers and block left open.
mistakes.consequence: Silicone bits lodge in the AVCS screens, oil control valves or bearing feeds, causing AVCS faults or oil starvation.
mistakes.prevent: Tape over the oil passages before scraping, then remove the tape and flush the passages with brake cleaner and air.

steps.title: Check AVCS sprocket lock state
steps.action: Before setting any marks, check whether the sensor plate on each cam sprocket turns freely against the sprocket housing.
steps.why: If an AVCS lock pin did not engage at shutdown, the sensor plate marks are meaningless and only the housing marks can be trusted.
steps.mistake: Timing to a free-floating sensor plate instead of the housing marks puts the cam out of time.

mistakes.title: Timed to a free-floating sensor plate
mistakes.what: Lining up the timing on the sensor plate mark of a sprocket whose plate turns freely.
mistakes.consequence: That camshaft goes back out of time, setting AVCS or correlation codes and bringing the cover off again.
mistakes.prevent: Check each plate for free movement and use the sprocket housing marks on any that are free.

mistakes.title: Free sensor plate not recorded
mistakes.what: Finding a free-turning sensor plate but not marking which sprocket it was.
mistakes.consequence: At reassembly that cam is timed to its sensor plate marks instead of the housing marks and ends up out of time.
mistakes.prevent: Tag any sprocket with a free plate and note it on the timing sheet so the housing marks are used at assembly.

steps.title: Align RH timing marks
steps.action: Turn the crank clockwise with the crankshaft socket until the crank sprocket and the RH intake and exhaust sprocket marks line up, with the crank key at six o'clock.

mistakes.title: Overshooting and backing up the crank
mistakes.what: Turning past the alignment point and reversing the crank a long way to come back.
mistakes.consequence: The chain slack moves to the wrong side and the marks look aligned when the cams are not where the procedure expects.
mistakes.prevent: Turn clockwise only, slowly near the marks, and go round again rather than backing up.

mistakes.title: Used chain not marked before removal
mistakes.what: Relying on the colored links of a used chain to show the timing at reassembly.
mistakes.consequence: The link colors fade or differ, so a reused chain can go back a tooth off.
mistakes.prevent: Paint-mark the chain links against each sprocket mark before removal, and note which bank each chain came from.

steps.title: Pin and remove RH tensioner
steps.action: Push the RH tensioner lever down, lock the plunger with a 2.5 mm pin or hex key in the stopper hole, then remove the tensioner and its lever.
steps.why: The plunger is spring and oil loaded; pinning it first keeps it from shooting out and lets it be reused.
tools: 2.5 mm stopper pin or hex key

mistakes.title: Tensioner removed unpinned
mistakes.what: Unbolting the RH tensioner without locking the plunger with the stopper pin.
mistakes.consequence: The plunger springs out, internal parts can be lost or damaged, and the tensioner may not be reusable.
mistakes.prevent: Push the lever down, lock the plunger with a 2.5 mm pin or hex key, and confirm it holds before removing the bolts.

steps.title: Remove RH chain and guide
steps.action: Unbolt the RH chain guide and lift off the RH timing chain, keeping RH parts separate from LH.
steps.why: With the chain off, both RH cams sit at zero lift and must only be turned within the range where they move freely by hand.
steps.mistake: Turning an untimed cam past its free range opens intake and exhaust valves together so they hit each other and bend.

mistakes.title: Untimed RH cam turned too far
mistakes.what: Turning an RH camshaft past the range where it moves freely by hand once the chain is off.
mistakes.consequence: Intake and exhaust valves open together and hit each other, bending valves.
mistakes.prevent: Only move an untimed cam within its free range; stop at any resistance.

mistakes.title: Bank parts mixed between sides
mistakes.what: Putting the RH chain and guides in the same box as the LH ones.
mistakes.consequence: The chains and guides are identical, so worn parts end up on the other bank against new wear surfaces, giving noise and faster wear.
mistakes.prevent: Bag and label chain, guides and tensioner by bank and note the chain running direction.

steps.title: Align LH timing marks
steps.action: Turn the crank to line up the crank key with the LH intake and exhaust sprocket marks.

mistakes.title: Expecting LH marks at RH positions
mistakes.what: Looking for the LH sprocket marks at the same clock positions as the RH and turning the crank past the real LH alignment.
mistakes.consequence: The LH chain comes off out of position, and a loaded cam may later be turned by mistake.
mistakes.prevent: Use the LH mark positions from the procedure, which differ from the RH positions.

steps.title: Pin and remove LH tensioner
steps.action: Push the LH tensioner lever down, pin the plunger, remove the tensioner and lever, and take the O-ring off the LH block half.

mistakes.title: LH tensioner O-ring left behind
mistakes.what: Leaving the old O-ring stuck in the LH block half when the tensioner comes out.
mistakes.consequence: A new O-ring is stacked on top at assembly and the joint leaks oil from the tensioner feed.
mistakes.prevent: Pick out the old O-ring now and bag it with the LH tensioner as a reminder to fit a new one.

steps.title: Remove LH chain and guide
steps.action: Unbolt the LH chain guide and lift off the LH timing chain.
steps.why: At this point the LH intake cam is holding its valves open and pistons 1 and 4 are near the top, so the LH intake cam must not be turned yet.
steps.mistake: Turning the LH intake cam now drives open valves into pistons 1 and 4.

mistakes.title: LH intake turned with pistons high
mistakes.what: Turning the LH intake cam right after the LH chain comes off.
mistakes.consequence: Its open valves are driven into pistons 1 and 4, which are near the top.
mistakes.prevent: Leave the LH intake cam alone until the pistons are parked at mid-stroke.

mistakes.title: Sensor plate bent while removing chain
mistakes.what: Levering the chain off with a screwdriver against the sprocket and its sensor plate.
mistakes.consequence: A bent sensor plate gives a wrong cam position signal, setting cam-to-crank correlation codes after the rebuild.
mistakes.prevent: Slacken the chain by hand once the guide is off and lift it straight away from the sprockets.
mistakes.detect: Cam and crank correlation codes, or AVCS values far from the reference, on the first drive.

steps.title: Park pistons at mid-stroke
steps.action: Turn the crankshaft about 200 degrees clockwise until the crank sprocket mark reaches the parked position, only backing up slightly to fine-tune.
steps.why: With all four pistons halfway down their bores, no valve can reach a piston, which makes it safe to turn the LH intake cam next.
steps.mistake: Turning the crank counterclockwise here can bring a piston up into an open valve.

mistakes.title: Crank reversed while parking pistons
mistakes.what: Turning the crank counterclockwise during the parking move.
mistakes.consequence: A piston can rise into an open LH intake valve and bend it.
mistakes.prevent: Turn clockwise only, and back up just slightly for the final adjustment.

mistakes.title: Pistons parked by eye
mistakes.what: Turning the crank roughly 200 degrees without checking the sprocket mark against its parked position.
mistakes.consequence: A piston is left near the top under the open LH intake valves, and turning that cam next bends them.
mistakes.prevent: Stop only when the crank sprocket mark sits at the parked position, and recheck it before touching the LH intake cam.

steps.title: Rotate LH intake to zero-lift
steps.action: Hold the LH intake sprocket with the pulley wrench and pin set and turn it about 180 degrees to its zero-lift mark.
steps.why: Every cam must sit at zero lift before the cam carriers are unbolted, or spring pressure loads the carrier unevenly.

mistakes.title: Overshooting the zero-lift mark
mistakes.what: Turning the LH intake sprocket past its zero-lift mark.
mistakes.consequence: The lobes start opening valves again, so spring load presses unevenly on the carrier when its bolts are loosened.
mistakes.prevent: Turn slowly with the pulley wrench and stop exactly on the mark.

mistakes.title: Cam turned on its sprocket bolt
mistakes.what: Turning the camshaft with a wrench on the sprocket bolt instead of the pulley wrench.
mistakes.consequence: The sprocket bolt loosens or the AVCS sprocket takes a load it was not designed for.
mistakes.prevent: Hold and turn the sprocket body with the pulley wrench and pin set.

steps.title: Remove the four cam sprockets
steps.action: Hold each sprocket with the pulley wrench and pin sets (a 6 mm rod through the RH exhaust sprocket), remove the bolts with the sprocket socket and tag each sprocket by position.
steps.why: The sprockets come off only when the carriers will be stripped; the camshafts must stay still while the bolts break loose.

mistakes.title: Sprockets not tagged by position
mistakes.what: Removing the four cam sprockets without marking which cam each came from.
mistakes.consequence: A sprocket goes back on the wrong cam, leading to AVCS faults or timing confusion and a second cover removal.
mistakes.prevent: Tag each sprocket RH or LH, intake or exhaust, as it comes off.

mistakes.title: AVCS sprocket dropped
mistakes.what: Dropping an AVCS sprocket on the floor or bench.
mistakes.consequence: The sensor plate bends or the internal lock pin is damaged, causing AVCS or correlation codes.
mistakes.prevent: Set sprockets down on a towel, plate side up, and inspect any that was dropped.

mistakes.title: Cam knock pin lost
mistakes.what: Letting the cam locating pin fall out unnoticed.
mistakes.consequence: The sprocket cannot be indexed to the cam at reassembly.
mistakes.prevent: Check each camshaft pin is present after the sprocket comes off.

steps.title: Remove both rocker covers
steps.action: Remove the intake manifold protectors and both rocker covers, then peel off the cover gaskets and spark plug tube gaskets.
steps.mistake: Scraping old sealant with the cam lobe under the scraper scores the lobe; turn the crank to move the lobe away first.

mistakes.title: Cam lobe scored while scraping
mistakes.what: Scraping old rocker cover sealant with a cam lobe sitting under the scraper.
mistakes.consequence: The lobe surface is scored and the camshaft has to be replaced.
mistakes.prevent: Turn the crank to move the lobe away from the area before scraping.

mistakes.title: Rocker cover pried at its flange
mistakes.what: Prying the rocker cover off at a corner of its flange.
mistakes.consequence: The flange bends and the new gasket leaks oil onto the exhaust.
mistakes.prevent: Lift evenly after all bolts are out, using a plastic tool only where the cover is stuck.

steps.title: Remove injectors and fuel pipes
steps.action: Unplug each injector, disconnect the fuel pipe quick connectors and unbolt each fuel pipe from its cam carrier with its injectors.

mistakes.title: Injector tips damaged
mistakes.what: Pulling injectors by their connectors or setting them down tip first.
mistakes.consequence: A damaged tip or body gives a poor spray or a leak after assembly.
mistakes.prevent: Lift each fuel pipe with its injectors as a unit and store the tips capped.

steps.title: Remove the water pipe assemblies
steps.action: Disconnect the water pipe hoses at the oil pan upper and remove the water pipe assemblies from each side.

mistakes.title: Old water pipe O-ring left in bore
mistakes.what: Leaving a flattened O-ring in its bore when the water pipe comes off.
mistakes.consequence: The new O-ring is stacked on the old one and the joint leaks coolant.
mistakes.prevent: Check every bore the pipes came out of and remove the old O-rings now.

steps.title: Tip engine RH cams up
steps.action: Extend the stand with steel rods and roll the engine onto its side so the RH camshafts face up.
steps.why: The rocker arms and shims are loose under the carrier; with the cams up they stay in place, and the extension rods keep the engine from toppling.

mistakes.title: Engine rolled without extension rods
mistakes.what: Rolling the engine onto its side on the stand without the steel extension rods fitted.
mistakes.consequence: The stand tips and the engine falls, cracking aluminum castings and endangering the technician.
mistakes.prevent: Fit the extension rods before rolling and check the stand is stable with the engine on its side.

mistakes.title: Cams facing down when carrier lifts
mistakes.what: Removing a cam carrier with that bank facing down.
mistakes.consequence: Rockers, pivots and shims fall out and get mixed up.
mistakes.prevent: Roll the engine so the bank being worked on faces up.

steps.title: Lift off RH cam carrier
steps.action: Loosen the RH carrier bolts evenly a little at a time in the factory loosening sequence and lift the carrier off with both camshafts in it.
steps.why: On the FB the camshafts are captured in the carrier; the carrier and cams come off as one unit.
steps.mistake: Loosening carrier bolts one at a time instead of evenly lets spring load bend or crack the carrier.

mistakes.title: Carrier bolts loosened one at a time
mistakes.what: Removing carrier bolts one by one instead of evenly across the carrier.
mistakes.consequence: Spring load concentrates on part of the carrier and bends or cracks it.
mistakes.prevent: Loosen every carrier bolt a little at a time in the factory loosening sequence.

mistakes.title: RH cam moved before carrier removal
mistakes.what: Turning an RH camshaft off zero lift while working near it, then loosening the carrier.
mistakes.consequence: The loaded lobe pushes the carrier unevenly as its bolts come out, which can crack it.
mistakes.prevent: Confirm both RH cams are still at zero lift immediately before loosening the carrier.

mistakes.title: Carrier pried at its corner
mistakes.what: Prying the cam carrier off at the cam cap corner.
mistakes.consequence: The cam cap cracks and the whole carrier has to be replaced.
mistakes.prevent: Break the sealant gently at several supported points with a plastic tool.

mistakes.title: Cam end caps disturbed
mistakes.what: Removing the small camshaft end cap covers that do not need to come off.
mistakes.consequence: The cap-to-carrier joint, a known leak point, is opened for no reason and needs its O-rings and sealant redone.
mistakes.prevent: Leave the end caps in place unless the carrier is being stripped.

steps.title: Bag RH rockers and shims
steps.action: Lift out the RH roller rockers, O-rings, valve shims and rocker pivots and store each in a labeled tray by valve.
steps.why: Each shim was selected for one valve; mixing them throws every cam clearance off.

mistakes.title: Rockers, pivots and shims mixed
mistakes.what: Dropping rockers, pivots and shims into one container.
mistakes.consequence: Every cam clearance changes, and worn rockers and pivots run against new partners, so the valvetrain has to be reshimmed.
mistakes.prevent: Use a labeled tray (an egg carton works) marked front, intake and exhaust, one per head.

mistakes.title: Shim missing from its valve
mistakes.what: Missing a shim stuck to the bottom of a rocker or fallen into the head.
mistakes.consequence: One valve ends up with no shim and a very large clearance, or a shim is doubled elsewhere.
mistakes.prevent: Count the shims against the valves before the head goes on the bench.
mistakes.detect: An empty slot in the tray or a clearance reading far outside the range.

steps.title: Lift off LH cam carrier
steps.action: Roll the engine LH cams up, loosen the LH carrier bolts evenly in sequence, lift off the carrier with its cams and bag the LH rockers, pivots and shims by position.

mistakes.title: LH cams loaded when carrier loosened
mistakes.what: Loosening the LH carrier without checking that both LH cams sit at zero lift.
mistakes.consequence: Uneven spring load bends or cracks the carrier as the bolts come out.
mistakes.prevent: Check the LH intake (turned earlier) and the LH exhaust are both at zero lift before the first bolt is loosened.

mistakes.title: LH and RH valvetrain trays mixed
mistakes.what: Putting LH rockers and shims in the tray already used for the RH side.
mistakes.consequence: Parts go back on the wrong head and every clearance on both sides is off.
mistakes.prevent: Use a separate labeled tray for each head.

steps.title: Loosen RH head bolts
steps.action: Loosen the RH head bolts evenly in the factory order, leaving bolts 1 and 4 threaded in three or four turns.
steps.why: Leaving two bolts engaged stops the head from dropping off the side of the block when the gasket lets go.

mistakes.title: Head bolts loosened out of order
mistakes.what: Breaking the head bolts loose randomly or one bolt fully at a time.
mistakes.consequence: The head distorts as clamp load is released unevenly, adding machining.
mistakes.prevent: Loosen in the factory order in small steps across all bolts.

mistakes.title: All head bolts pulled at once
mistakes.what: Removing every head bolt before the gasket has let go.
mistakes.consequence: The head drops off the side of the block when it breaks free, nicking the deck or the head face.
mistakes.prevent: Leave bolts 1 and 4 threaded in a few turns until the head is loose.

steps.title: Remove the RH head
steps.action: Tap the RH head loose with a plastic hammer, remove the last two bolts and lift the head and gasket off without scratching either face.

mistakes.title: Screwdriver in the head joint
mistakes.what: Prying between the head and block to break the gasket.
mistakes.consequence: Both sealing faces are gouged, which means resurfacing or a new head gasket leak.
mistakes.prevent: Tap the head loose with a plastic hammer at its solid points.

mistakes.title: Head laid on its gasket face
mistakes.what: Setting the head face down on a dirty bench.
mistakes.consequence: The gasket face is scratched by grit or hardware on the bench.
mistakes.prevent: Lay the head on its side on wood blocks or a clean towel.

mistakes.title: Old head gasket not inspected
mistakes.what: Throwing away the old head gasket without looking at it.
mistakes.consequence: Tracks showing gas or coolant crossing the gasket, which point to a warped face or crack, are lost.
mistakes.prevent: Look over the gasket at the fire rings and coolant holes before scrapping it.

steps.title: Remove the LH head
steps.action: Loosen the LH head bolts in order, keep bolts 1 and 4 engaged, tap the head free and lift it off with its gasket.

mistakes.title: Coolant runs into LH bores
mistakes.what: Lifting the LH head with coolant still in its jackets.
mistakes.consequence: Coolant pours into the open bores and crankcase and starts corroding liners and bearing surfaces.
mistakes.prevent: Drain what you can first, mop up immediately, and wipe and oil the liners.

steps.title: Strip the cam carriers
steps.action: Loosen the cam cap bolts evenly in sequence, keep the caps in order, lift out the camshafts and pull the AVCS filter screens.
steps.why: The caps are machined in place with the carrier and must return to their original positions.

mistakes.title: Cam caps mixed or reversed
mistakes.what: Removing cam caps without marking their positions and direction.
mistakes.consequence: A cap in the wrong place does not match the line bore, so the cam binds or the clearance is wrong.
mistakes.prevent: Mark every cap and lay them out in order; the caps and carrier are only serviced as a set.

mistakes.title: Removed AVCS screen reused
mistakes.what: Pushing a removed AVCS filter screen back in.
mistakes.consequence: A disturbed screen may not seal or may sit rotated, restricting oil to the AVCS sprocket.
mistakes.prevent: Treat a removed screen as scrap and fit a new one at assembly.

steps.title: Remove valves and springs
steps.action: Compress each spring, remove the collets, then the retainer, spring, valve and spring seat, keeping each valve's parts together.

mistakes.title: Valve parts mixed between valves
mistakes.what: Collecting all retainers, springs and valves in one pile.
mistakes.consequence: Valves end up in different guides and seats from the ones they wore into, so they leak or need extra seat work.
mistakes.prevent: Keep each valve with its spring, retainer and collets in a numbered rack.

mistakes.title: Valve forced past a burred tip
mistakes.what: Pushing a valve out through its guide with a mushroomed or burred stem tip.
mistakes.consequence: The burr scores the guide bore and the guide has to be replaced.
mistakes.prevent: Dress any burr on the stem tip with a fine stone before sliding the valve out.

mistakes.title: Compressor slips off the retainer
mistakes.what: Using a spring compressor that is not square to the retainer.
mistakes.consequence: It slips, the collets fly and can be lost, and the retainer or head is marked.
mistakes.prevent: Center the compressor on the retainer and compress only enough to free the collets.

steps.title: Pull stem seals and studs
steps.action: Remove the valve stem seals from the guides and the stud bolts and chain cover bolt from the heads.

mistakes.title: Valve guide damaged pulling seals
mistakes.what: Gripping the stem seal with pliers that also bite the top of the guide.
mistakes.consequence: A marked or cracked guide lets the new seal leak, which raises oil consumption.
mistakes.prevent: Use a seal removal tool or pliers that grip only the seal body.

steps.title: Remove the crank sprocket
steps.action: Slide the crank sprocket off the crankshaft nose.

mistakes.title: Sprocket pried against block face
mistakes.what: Levering the crank sprocket off against the front face of the block.
mistakes.consequence: The chain cover sealing face on the block is gouged.
mistakes.prevent: Slide the sprocket off by hand or with a puller that bears on the crank nose.

mistakes.title: Crank key lost
mistakes.what: Letting the crank key fall out unnoticed.
mistakes.consequence: The sprocket cannot be timed until a key is found or replaced.
mistakes.prevent: Check the key after the sprocket comes off and bag it.

steps.title: Remove block-mounted ancillaries
steps.action: Remove the rear engine hanger, the water pipe and PCV connector set with their O-rings, the knock sensor and the PCV valve.

mistakes.title: Knock sensor dropped or pried
mistakes.what: Prying the knock sensor off or letting it drop.
mistakes.consequence: A damaged sensor reports knock poorly, so the ignition is not retarded when it should be.
mistakes.prevent: Unbolt it and lift it straight off; replace any sensor that has been dropped.

mistakes.title: Old O-rings left in the bosses
mistakes.what: Leaving PCV connector or water pipe O-rings stuck in their bores.
mistakes.consequence: New O-rings are stacked on old ones at assembly and the joint leaks.
mistakes.prevent: Check each bore after removal and pick out any O-ring left behind.

steps.title: Remove drive plate and sensor
steps.action: Unbolt the drive plate with its crank position sensor plate, then remove the crank position sensor and holder from the LH half.

mistakes.title: Crank sensor plate bent
mistakes.what: Laying the drive plate down on its sensor plate teeth or stacking parts on it.
mistakes.consequence: Bent teeth give an erratic crank signal and misfire or no-start codes.
mistakes.prevent: Store the drive plate flat on a clean surface with the sensor plate up.

mistakes.title: Crank sensor tip damaged
mistakes.what: Prying the crank position sensor out or leaving its tip exposed to metal chips.
mistakes.consequence: A cracked tip or one coated with metal particles gives a weak crank signal.
mistakes.prevent: Unbolt and lift the sensor straight out, clean the tip and store it bagged.

steps.title: Remove thermostat and water pump
steps.action: Turn the block oil pan up, take it off the stand, then remove the thermostat cover and thermostat and the water pump from the oil pan upper.
steps.why: Both are mounted on the oil pan upper, which comes off next.

mistakes.title: Water pump pried at its gasket face
mistakes.what: Prying the water pump off the oil pan upper at the gasket joint.
mistakes.consequence: The pump mounting face on the oil pan upper is gouged and leaks coolant later.
mistakes.prevent: Tap the pump loose with a plastic hammer after all bolts are out.

steps.title: Remove oil pan upper
steps.action: Unbolt the oil pan upper and lift it off together with the lower pan, then take the O-ring off the block; if the lower pan must be separated, cut its sealant with an oil pan cutter.
steps.why: The rod caps are reached through the bottom of the block, so the pans have to come off before any piston can come out.
steps.mistake: Prying the lower pan off with a screwdriver bends the flange and gouges the sealing face.

mistakes.title: Lower pan pried with a screwdriver
mistakes.what: Prying the lower oil pan off at its flange with a screwdriver.
mistakes.consequence: The thin flange bends and its sealing face is gouged, so it leaks after assembly.
mistakes.prevent: Cut the sealant with an oil pan cutter and lift the pan off evenly.

mistakes.title: Upper pan pried at block seam
mistakes.what: Driving a screwdriver into the oil pan upper to block joint.
mistakes.consequence: This joint is a known FB leak point, and a gouge there seeps oil after the rebuild.
mistakes.prevent: Break the sealant with an oil pan cutter or plastic tools and lift evenly.

mistakes.title: Strainer and pan not inspected
mistakes.what: Washing the oil pan and strainer before looking at what is in them.
mistakes.consequence: Debris that explains an AVCS or bearing failure is washed away unseen.
mistakes.prevent: Look at the strainer screen and pan bottom first and keep any debris for diagnosis.
mistakes.detect: Bearing material, sealant bits or sludge on the strainer screen.

steps.title: Stand block on its rear
steps.action: Thread four same-length bolts into the A/C compressor and generator bracket holes as feet, then stand the block with the rear seal down.
steps.why: The bolts keep the dowel (knock) pins off the bench, and standing the block up lets the pistons come straight out of the bores.

mistakes.title: Block balanced on uneven feet
mistakes.what: Using four bolts of different lengths as feet, so the block rocks.
mistakes.consequence: The block tips while pistons are being pushed out, bending dowel pins or nicking the rear seal face.
mistakes.prevent: Use four identical bolts and check the block sits solidly before working on it.

steps.title: Remove rods 1 and 4
steps.action: Turn the crank to bring the 1 and 4 rod caps into reach, remove each cap and bolt with the rod socket, rotate the crank to clear each pin, and push each piston and rod out the top of its bore.
steps.why: The FB has no piston pin service holes; its diagonally split rods let the piston and rod leave through the bore once the head is off.
steps.mistake: Letting the rod's big end drag along the bore scratches the liner; guide it out by hand.

mistakes.title: Big end drags down the liner
mistakes.what: Pushing the piston out and letting the rod big end scrape along the bore.
mistakes.consequence: The cast iron liner is scratched, which can mean honing or boring that would not otherwise be needed.
mistakes.prevent: Guide the rod by hand so the big end stays centered as the piston leaves the bore.

mistakes.title: Crank turned with rod cap off
mistakes.what: Rotating the crank while a rod cap is off and the rod is still on its pin.
mistakes.consequence: The loose big end swings and nicks the crank pin or the bottom of the liner.
mistakes.prevent: Guide each rod clear of the pin by hand as the crank turns.

mistakes.title: Rod bolt heads rounded
mistakes.what: Using a generic socket on the rod bolts in the cramped pan opening.
mistakes.consequence: The bolt head rounds and the cap is hard to remove without damage.
mistakes.prevent: Use the rod bolt socket specified for the FB and keep it square to the bolt.

steps.title: Remove rods 2 and 3
steps.action: Rotate the crank to reach the 2 and 3 caps, remove them and push those piston and rod assemblies out, marking every cap and piston with its cylinder number.
steps.mistake: Mixing rod caps between rods ruins the bore geometry; each cap only fits its own rod.

mistakes.title: Rod caps mixed between rods
mistakes.what: Removing caps without marking them and fitting them back to the wrong rods.
mistakes.consequence: Each cap is machined with its own rod, so a swapped cap leaves the big end bore out of shape.
mistakes.prevent: Mark every cap and rod with its cylinder number as they come apart.

mistakes.title: Old bearing shells not kept in order
mistakes.what: Throwing the rod bearing shells in one bag.
mistakes.consequence: The wear pattern on each shell, which shows dirt, misalignment or starvation, can no longer be matched to its position.
mistakes.prevent: Lay the old shells out by cylinder and upper or lower position and read them before scrapping.

steps.title: Unbolt the block halves
steps.action: Lay the block RH half up on a padded board, remove the single outer joining bolt, then loosen the joining bolts in the factory order.
steps.why: The padded board protects the dowel pins and keeps the block stable while it is split.

mistakes.title: Joining bolts loosened out of order
mistakes.what: Loosening the block joining bolts in random order or fully one at a time.
mistakes.consequence: The halves and main bores distort as load comes off unevenly.
mistakes.prevent: Follow the factory loosening order in steps across all bolts.

mistakes.title: Outer joining bolt forgotten
mistakes.what: Trying to separate the halves with the single outer joining bolt still fitted.
mistakes.consequence: The block halves are levered against the bolt and a flange can crack.
mistakes.prevent: Remove the outer bolt first and check all bolt holes are empty before lifting.

steps.title: Split the block halves
steps.action: Lift the RH half a little, confirm the crankshaft is staying in the LH half, then lift the RH half clear.
steps.why: The crank can stick to the upper half and fall out if the half is lifted quickly.
steps.mistake: Lifting the RH half in one pull lets the crank drop and nick journals or the mating faces.

mistakes.title: RH half lifted in one pull
mistakes.what: Lifting the RH block half quickly without checking where the crank is staying.
mistakes.consequence: The crank sticks to the RH half, then drops and nicks its journals or the mating faces.
mistakes.prevent: Lift a little, confirm the crank is staying in the LH half, then lift clear.

mistakes.title: Halves pried apart at the seam
mistakes.what: Driving a tool into the parting line to break the sealant.
mistakes.consequence: The gouged faces leak, and because the halves are machined as a pair, damage cannot be fixed by replacing one half.
mistakes.prevent: Lift slowly and evenly, using plastic tools only at supported points.

mistakes.title: Main shells fall out mixed
mistakes.what: Letting the main bearing shells drop out of the RH half and get mixed.
mistakes.consequence: Their wear pattern can no longer be read by position.
mistakes.prevent: Lay the RH half down carefully and collect the shells in order.

steps.title: Lift out the crankshaft
steps.action: Lift the crankshaft out of the LH half, pull the rear main seal and the LH O-ring, and push out the main bearings from the end opposite the locating lip, keeping them in order.

mistakes.title: Crank set down on its journals
mistakes.what: Laying the crank on a steel bench or letting it roll.
mistakes.consequence: Journals are nicked or the crank bent, which adds grinding or a new crank.
mistakes.prevent: Stand the crank on end or support it in V-blocks on wood.

steps.title: Strip block plugs and covers
steps.action: Remove the water jacket spacers, the oil separator cover, the block plug and main gallery plugs from both halves, and the block plate from the LH half.
steps.why: The galleries can only be cleaned properly with every plug out.

mistakes.title: Gallery plugs left in for cleaning
mistakes.what: Washing the block halves without removing the main gallery plugs and block plug.
mistakes.consequence: Sludge and debris stay in the galleries and break loose into the new bearings on first start.
mistakes.prevent: Remove every plug so the galleries can be brushed and flushed end to end.

mistakes.title: Gallery plug hex rounded
mistakes.what: Using a worn hex bit or ratchet that cams out on a tight plug.
mistakes.consequence: The plug rounds and has to be drilled out, putting chips into the gallery.
mistakes.prevent: Use a good hex bit fully seated, with heat if needed, and clean thoroughly if drilling is unavoidable.

steps.title: Disassemble pistons from rods
steps.action: Remove the rod bearings, take the rings off top first, then the oil rails and expander, pry out one circlip with a taped screwdriver, push out the pin and separate the rod.
steps.why: Keeping rings, pins and rods together by cylinder matters if any are reused.

mistakes.title: Piston pin hammered out
mistakes.what: Driving the pin out with a drift and hammer.
mistakes.consequence: The piston pin bore or the rod bushing distorts, so a reused piston no longer fits its pin.
mistakes.prevent: Pins should push out by hand at room temperature; if one will not, find out why.

mistakes.title: Circlip groove gouged
mistakes.what: Prying circlips out with a bare screwdriver that cuts into the groove.
mistakes.consequence: A burred groove stops the new circlip seating, and a loose clip can let the pin walk into the bore.
mistakes.prevent: Tape the screwdriver tip and lever against the clip only; check grooves for burrs afterward.

mistakes.title: Rings spiraled off reusable pistons
mistakes.what: Winding the old rings off by hand on pistons that will be reused.
mistakes.consequence: The ring ends scratch the ring lands and skirt coating.
mistakes.prevent: Use a ring expander for removal too when the pistons are to be reused.

steps.title: Clean parts and passages
steps.action: Strip all old liquid gasket with plastic scrapers and remover, wash every part and blow out the oil and coolant passages.
steps.why: Measuring dirty parts gives false readings, and a blocked gallery starves a bearing.

mistakes.title: Oil galleries not brushed out
mistakes.what: Washing the block and crank without running brushes through every oil gallery and drilling.
mistakes.consequence: Hidden sludge or machining debris breaks loose on first start and is carried straight into the new bearings.
mistakes.prevent: Brush every gallery and crank oil hole, wash with hot water and detergent, then blow dry.
mistakes.detect: A clean white rag pushed through a gallery comes out dirty.

mistakes.title: Abrasive pads used on parts
mistakes.what: Cleaning sealing faces or bearing surfaces with abrasive pads or discs.
mistakes.consequence: Abrasive grit embeds in the aluminum and washes into the oil passages, and sealing faces lose their flatness.
mistakes.prevent: Use gasket remover, plastic scrapers and detergent; never abrasives on sealing or bearing surfaces.

mistakes.title: Carrier and head oil lines skipped
mistakes.what: Cleaning the outside of the cam carriers and heads but not checking their internal oil lines.
mistakes.consequence: Old contamination left in the AVCS feed reaches the sprocket and oil control valve and sets AVCS codes.
mistakes.prevent: Flush and blow through each carrier and head oil line and look for clogs, as the AVCS bulletin directs.

mistakes.title: Liners left wet after washing
mistakes.what: Leaving the washed block to air dry without oiling the cast iron liners.
mistakes.consequence: Flash rust forms on the liners and has to be honed off again.
mistakes.prevent: Blow the bores dry immediately and wipe them with clean engine oil.

steps.title: Crack-check heads and block
steps.action: Look over the heads and block for cracks and use dye penetrant on the critical areas, and check gasket faces for gas or water tracks.

mistakes.title: Crack check skipped after overheating
mistakes.what: Assuming a head is fine because it looks clean, on an engine with an overheating history.
mistakes.consequence: A crack between seats or into a water jacket leaks coolant or compression after the rebuild.
mistakes.prevent: Dye-check the combustion chambers and gasket faces of any head that has overheated.

mistakes.title: Dye penetrant on dirty surfaces
mistakes.what: Applying dye over carbon, oil or sealant residue.
mistakes.consequence: The dye cannot enter a crack, so the test gives a false pass.
mistakes.prevent: Clean and degrease the area to bare metal before applying dye.

steps.title: Measure head deck warpage
steps.action: Check each head's block face with a straightedge and feeler gauge across the factory positions at room temperature.
steps.why: A warped head face will not clamp evenly even if every bolt is torqued correctly.

mistakes.title: Warpage measured over residue
mistakes.what: Laying the straightedge across faces that still carry sealant or burrs.
mistakes.consequence: The reading is wrong in either direction, so a good head is machined or a warped one is reused.
mistakes.prevent: Measure only on fully cleaned faces at room temperature.

mistakes.title: Warpage checked lengthwise only
mistakes.what: Measuring along the head but not across it and on the diagonals.
mistakes.consequence: A twisted face passes the check and the gasket leaks once torqued.
mistakes.prevent: Check every factory position, including across and diagonally.

steps.title: Measure stem-to-guide clearance
steps.action: Measure each valve stem in six places and each guide bore in six places and subtract, also checking the valve margin thickness.

mistakes.title: Guide measured at one depth
mistakes.what: Measuring the guide bore at a single point.
mistakes.consequence: Bell-mouth wear at the guide ends is missed and the valve rocks, wearing the new stem seal and raising oil use.
mistakes.prevent: Measure stems and guides in six places as the procedure specifies.

mistakes.title: Thin valve margin reused
mistakes.what: Reusing a valve whose margin is at or below the limit.
mistakes.consequence: The thin edge overheats and can burn, losing compression in that cylinder.
mistakes.prevent: Measure every margin and replace valves that are under the limit.

steps.title: Check shim fit on stems
steps.action: Measure each valve stem tip and the bore of its shim and confirm the clearance between them.

mistakes.title: Shim fit to stem not checked
mistakes.what: Assuming any shim fits any stem tip without measuring the clearance between them.
mistakes.consequence: An over-loose shim can move on the stem tip, changing cam clearance and wearing the tip.
mistakes.prevent: Measure each stem tip and its shim bore and compare with the limit.

steps.title: Check valve seat contact
steps.action: Dye each valve face, press it onto its seat without turning, and measure the contact width and where it lands on the face.
steps.why: The contact band should sit in the middle of the valve face; a wide or off-center band means the seats need cutting.

spec.note: intake seat width; exhaust 1.1 to 1.7 mm

mistakes.title: Valve turned during dye check
mistakes.what: Spinning the valve on its seat while checking the contact pattern.
mistakes.consequence: The dye smears into a band that looks continuous even when the seat is poor.
mistakes.prevent: Press the valve straight onto its seat without turning it.

mistakes.title: Off-center seat band accepted
mistakes.what: Passing a contact band that sits at the edge of the valve face.
mistakes.consequence: The valve seals and cools poorly and can leak or burn.
mistakes.prevent: The band must sit centered on the face and within width; recut the seat if not.

steps.title: Test the valve springs
steps.action: Check each spring's free length, load at installed and open height, and squareness on a surface plate.

spec.note: free length; squareness 2.5 deg / 1.8 mm max

mistakes.title: Springs checked for length only
mistakes.what: Measuring free length but not load or squareness.
mistakes.consequence: A weak or leaning spring lets the valve float or bounce at high rpm, damaging the seat and valve.
mistakes.prevent: Check free length, load at installed and open height, and squareness on a surface plate.

steps.title: Measure camshaft lobes and runout
steps.action: Check camshaft bend with a dial gauge on V-blocks, and measure lobe height, base circle and journal diameters.

spec.note: intake lobe height; exhaust 40.15 to 40.25 mm; bend limit 0.020 mm

mistakes.title: Cam checked against wrong year spec
mistakes.what: Using lobe heights from a different FB25 version when deciding if a cam is worn.
mistakes.consequence: Lobe heights changed between versions, so a good cam is scrapped or a worn one is passed.
mistakes.prevent: Use the spec for the exact engine version (check STIS by VIN), not a later Legacy figure.

mistakes.title: Scored cam journals reused
mistakes.what: Reusing a camshaft whose journals are scratched.
mistakes.consequence: Journal drag slows the AVCS response and sets slow-response codes.
mistakes.prevent: Inspect every journal; scored cams and carriers are replaced as the AVCS bulletin directs.
mistakes.detect: One camshaft turns noticeably stiffer in the carrier than the others.

steps.title: Plastigage cam journal clearance
steps.action: Lay Plastigage across each cam journal, torque the caps in sequence, remove them and read the widest point; also check cam end play with a dial gauge.
steps.why: If clearance is out, the caps and carrier are replaced as a set because they are line-bored together.

spec.note: oil clearance; caps at 18 N·m; thrust 0.068 to 0.116 mm

mistakes.title: Cam turned with Plastigage in place
mistakes.what: Rotating the camshaft after the caps are torqued on the Plastigage.
mistakes.consequence: The crushed strip smears around the journal and the cam clearance reading is useless.
mistakes.prevent: Hold the cam still while the caps are torqued and removed.

mistakes.title: Plastigage on an oily journal
mistakes.what: Laying the strip on a journal still wet with oil.
mistakes.consequence: The strip sticks or spreads and gives a wrong width.
mistakes.prevent: Wipe the journal and cap clean where the strip will sit.

mistakes.title: Plastigage residue left behind
mistakes.what: Scraping the crushed strip off with a hard tool, or leaving bits on the cap.
mistakes.consequence: The journal or cap is scratched, or residue sits under the cap at assembly.
mistakes.prevent: Remove the strip carefully with a clean rag; it dissolves in oil, but wipe it off anyway.

mistakes.title: Single cap replaced on carrier
mistakes.what: Fitting a replacement cam cap to an existing carrier to fix one bad clearance.
mistakes.consequence: The cap is not line-bored with the carrier, so the journal clearance is uneven and the cam can bind.
mistakes.prevent: Replace the caps and carrier together as a set when clearance is out.

steps.title: Inspect timing chain parts
steps.action: Check both chains, guides, tensioner levers, tensioners and all sprocket teeth for cracks or abnormal wear, and confirm the crank sprocket has no play on its key.

mistakes.title: Worn guides reused with new chain
mistakes.what: Fitting a new chain against chain guides that already have grooves worn into them.
mistakes.consequence: The chain runs noisy and the tensioner runs out of travel sooner, bringing the cover off again.
mistakes.prevent: Replace guides that show grooving or cracks; the tensioner notch count at assembly reflects wear.

mistakes.title: Faulty AVCS sprocket reused
mistakes.what: Reinstalling the original sprockets and oil control valves on an engine that had AVCS codes.
mistakes.consequence: The contamination or wear that set the codes is still in the sprocket, so the codes return.
mistakes.prevent: If the history shows AVCS codes, follow the AVCS bulletins and replace the sprocket or valve they identify.

mistakes.title: Crank sprocket play ignored
mistakes.what: Accepting a crank sprocket that rocks on its key.
mistakes.consequence: The sprocket can shift under load, moving the timing on both banks.
mistakes.prevent: Check for play on the key and replace the sprocket or key if there is any.

steps.title: Measure block deck warpage
steps.action: Check both head faces of the block with a straightedge and feeler gauge.

mistakes.title: Thread pull-up missed at bolt holes
mistakes.what: Checking the deck with a straightedge but ignoring raised metal around the head bolt holes.
mistakes.consequence: A raised ring of metal holds the gasket off the deck there and the head gasket can leak.
mistakes.prevent: Run a flat stone lightly over the decks and chamfer any raised thread entry before measuring.

steps.title: Bore-gauge all four cylinders
steps.action: Measure each liner at four depths (10, 45, 80 and 115 mm) in both the thrust and pin directions and work out size, taper and out-of-round.
steps.why: The bore size grade (A or B) is stamped on the block deck and decides which piston grade belongs in each hole.

mistakes.title: Bores measured in one direction
mistakes.what: Measuring only across the thrust direction.
mistakes.consequence: Out-of-round wear is missed and the rings never seal fully, raising oil consumption.
mistakes.prevent: Measure at four depths in both the thrust and pin directions.

mistakes.title: Bore grade stamp ignored
mistakes.what: Ordering or fitting pistons without reading the A or B grade stamped on the deck.
mistakes.consequence: The wrong grade puts piston-to-wall clearance out of range, giving piston slap or scuffing.
mistakes.prevent: Record the stamped grade for each bore and match the piston grade to it.

steps.title: Calculate piston-to-wall clearance
steps.action: Measure each piston across the thrust faces 13.3 mm up from the skirt bottom and subtract from its bore size.

mistakes.title: Piston measured at wrong height
mistakes.what: Measuring the piston somewhere other than 13.3 mm up from the skirt bottom.
mistakes.consequence: The calculated piston-to-wall clearance is wrong, so a loose or tight fit is passed.
mistakes.prevent: Mark the measuring height on the skirt and use the thrust faces only.

mistakes.title: Pistons matched to wrong bores
mistakes.what: Calculating clearance with each piston against a different bore than it will go into.
mistakes.consequence: Each final pairing can be out of range even though every calculation looked fine.
mistakes.prevent: Number pistons to their bores before measuring and keep them paired.

steps.title: Check piston pin fit
steps.action: Confirm each pin pushes into its piston with thumb pressure at room temperature, measure pin bore and pin, and check the circlip grooves for burrs.

mistakes.title: Tight pin forced in
mistakes.what: Hammering or pressing a pin that will not push in by thumb at room temperature.
mistakes.consequence: The pin bore distorts, and the pin can seize or score its bore.
mistakes.prevent: A pin should enter with thumb pressure; measure and correct any that will not.

mistakes.title: Pins swapped between pistons
mistakes.what: Mixing pins between pistons after measuring them.
mistakes.consequence: Each pin now sits in a bore it was not measured with, so the recorded fit no longer applies.
mistakes.prevent: Keep each pin bagged with its own piston and rod from measuring onward.

steps.title: Measure ring end gaps
steps.action: Square each ring in its bore with a piston and measure the gap with a feeler gauge.

spec.note: top ring; second 0.30 to 0.45; oil rails 0.20 to 0.50

mistakes.title: Ring end gap not checked
mistakes.what: Fitting rings straight from the box without measuring their gaps in the bore.
mistakes.consequence: A gap that is too tight closes when hot, the ring ends butt, and the ring breaks or scuffs the liner and lands.
mistakes.prevent: Check every ring in the bore it will run in before it goes on the piston.

mistakes.title: Ring cocked in the bore
mistakes.what: Measuring the gap with the ring tilted in the bore.
mistakes.consequence: The gap reads wrong, hiding a tight or wide ring.
mistakes.prevent: Push the ring down with an inverted piston so it sits square before measuring.

mistakes.title: Wrong year ring gap spec
mistakes.what: Judging gaps against the figures for a different FB25 ring set.
mistakes.consequence: The ring set changed with the oil control ring update and later engines, so good rings are rejected or out-of-spec rings accepted.
mistakes.prevent: Match the gap spec to the ring set actually being fitted and check STIS by VIN.

steps.title: Measure ring side clearance
steps.action: Clean the ring grooves, roll each compression ring in its groove and measure the side clearance with a feeler gauge.

mistakes.title: Ring grooves left carboned
mistakes.what: Measuring side clearance or refitting reused pistons without cleaning the grooves.
mistakes.consequence: Carbon holds the ring and gives a false reading; a ring that sticks in its groove passes oil.
mistakes.prevent: Clean every groove back to bare metal, including the oil ring drain holes.

mistakes.title: Groove gouged while cleaning
mistakes.what: Cleaning grooves with a tool that cuts into the groove sides.
mistakes.consequence: A damaged groove lets the ring flutter and leak, so the piston must be replaced.
mistakes.prevent: Use a proper groove cleaner or a broken ring of the right width, with light pressure.

steps.title: Check rods for bend
steps.action: Check each rod for bend and twist on a rod aligner and look over the thrust faces and small-end bushing.

spec.note: bend or twist limit per 100 mm

mistakes.title: Rod from a failed bearing reused
mistakes.what: Reusing a rod from a cylinder with a spun or burned bearing without checking it on an aligner.
mistakes.consequence: A bent or twisted rod loads the new bearing on its edges and wears it out early.
mistakes.prevent: Check every rod for bend and twist, and look hard at any from a failed bearing.
mistakes.detect: Bearing wear concentrated on opposite edges of the two shells.

mistakes.title: Dropped rod reused
mistakes.what: Reusing a rod that was dropped during teardown.
mistakes.consequence: A bent or nicked rod causes the same edge loading and early bearing failure.
