mistakes.prevent: Recheck any dropped rod on the aligner and inspect it for nicks.

steps.title: Measure pin-to-bushing clearance
steps.action: Measure the piston pin and the rod small-end bushing and subtract.

mistakes.title: Bushing measured in one place
mistakes.what: Measuring the small-end bushing in a single direction.
mistakes.consequence: Oval wear in the bushing is missed and the loose pin knocks once the engine runs.
mistakes.prevent: Measure the bushing in more than one direction and at both ends.

steps.title: Check rod side clearance
steps.action: Fit each rod and cap to the crank with a new oiled bolt, tighten to the full rod bolt procedure while holding the crank, and measure side play with a feeler gauge.
steps.why: Side clearance is only meaningful with the cap at full clamp, and the rod bolts are stretched in doing it.

mistakes.title: Checking bolts reused for final assembly
mistakes.what: Measuring side clearance with new rod bolts torqued and angled, then using those same bolts for the final build.
mistakes.consequence: The bolts have already been stretched once, so they clamp less and a cap can loosen and spin a bearing.
mistakes.prevent: Keep the checking bolts separate and use a fresh set of rod bolts for final assembly.

mistakes.title: Side clearance read with snug bolts
mistakes.what: Measuring rod side play with the bolts only snugged.
mistakes.consequence: The side play reading does not represent the rod as it will run under full clamp.
mistakes.prevent: Measure only after the full rod bolt procedure, as the step requires.

mistakes.title: Rod fitted reversed on the pin
mistakes.what: Fitting a diagonally split rod with its side faces reversed on the crank pin.
mistakes.consequence: The offset rod and bearing sit wrong on the journal and wear unevenly.
mistakes.prevent: Check rod orientation marks against the factory figure before measuring.

steps.title: Plastigage rod bearing clearance
steps.action: Lay Plastigage across each crank pin, fit the rod and cap with a new bolt and full rod bolt torque without letting the rod move, then remove the cap and read the strip.
steps.why: This is the only check of the actual oil film the rod bearing will run on.
steps.mistake: Turning the crank with Plastigage in place smears it and gives a false reading.

mistakes.title: Crank turned with Plastigage on pin
mistakes.what: Rotating the crankshaft while the rod cap is torqued on the Plastigage.
mistakes.consequence: The strip smears and gives a false rod clearance reading.
mistakes.prevent: Hold the crank still from torquing until the cap is off again.

mistakes.title: Plastigage on an oiled crank pin
mistakes.what: Laying the strip on a pin that still has oil on it.
mistakes.consequence: The strip spreads or sticks and gives a false width.
mistakes.prevent: Wipe the pin and shell dry where the strip goes.

mistakes.title: Strip read at one spot only
mistakes.what: Reading only the widest point and ignoring changes along the strip.
mistakes.consequence: Taper along the crank pin or the bearing goes unnoticed and that bearing wears unevenly.
mistakes.prevent: Read along the full length and note the high and low readings.

mistakes.title: Strip range does not cover spec
mistakes.what: Using a Plastigage size whose range does not reach the low end of the rod clearance spec.
mistakes.consequence: The narrowest Clevite strip starts at 0.025 mm, so clearances near the 0.017 mm minimum cannot be read accurately.
mistakes.prevent: Use the smallest range strip and confirm tight readings with a bore gauge and micrometer.

mistakes.title: Plastigage used instead of measuring
mistakes.what: Relying on Plastigage alone without miking the pins and bores first.
mistakes.consequence: Out-of-round pins or bores pass because Plastigage only shows the vertical clearance.
mistakes.prevent: Measure journals and housing bores with mics and gauges first, then use Plastigage as the final check.

steps.title: Measure crankshaft journals and runout
steps.action: Crack-check the crank, check runout on the end journals with a dial gauge, and mic every main journal and crank pin for size, taper and out-of-round.

spec.note: runout limit; pins and journals 0.005 mm out-of-round, 0.006 mm cylindricality

mistakes.title: Journals miked in one plane
mistakes.what: Measuring each journal and pin at only one point.
mistakes.consequence: Out-of-round and taper beyond the small FB limits are missed.
mistakes.prevent: Measure each journal at both ends and at two angles.

mistakes.title: Crack check skipped after spun bearing
mistakes.what: Reusing a crank from an engine that spun a bearing without crack-checking it.
mistakes.consequence: A heat-affected journal can carry a crack that later breaks the crank.
mistakes.prevent: Crack-check any crank that has run a failed bearing, and again after any regrind.

steps.title: Measure crankshaft end play
steps.action: With all main bearings in the block and the crank laid in, measure end play at the number 5 thrust bearing with a feeler gauge.

spec.note: thrust is taken by the #5 main bearing

mistakes.title: Thrust bearing in the wrong position
mistakes.what: Fitting a plain shell at #5 and the flanged thrust bearing elsewhere.
mistakes.consequence: The crank has no proper thrust control, wears its thrust faces and the block, and destroys the case.
mistakes.prevent: Confirm the flanged thrust shells sit in the #5 position before measuring end play.

mistakes.title: End play read without full travel
mistakes.what: Measuring without pushing the crank fully forward and back.
mistakes.consequence: End play reads smaller than it really is, hiding a worn thrust face on the crank.
mistakes.prevent: Lever the crank fully each way and measure at the #5 thrust bearing.

steps.title: Plastigage main bearing clearance
steps.action: Lay Plastigage on each journal, join the block halves with oiled bolts and run the full joining-bolt torque sequence, then split the halves and read each strip.
steps.why: Main clearance can only be read with the two halves clamped exactly as they will run.
steps.mistake: Checking mains with only a few bolts snug gives a reading that is too loose.

mistakes.title: Mains checked with bolts only snug
mistakes.what: Joining the halves for the main clearance check with only some bolts snugged.
mistakes.consequence: The halves are not clamped as they will run, so the clearance reads too loose.
mistakes.prevent: Run the full joining bolt sequence before reading the strips.

mistakes.title: Joining bolts prepared wrong
mistakes.what: Torquing the joining bolts with dirty threads or without the specified light oil.
mistakes.consequence: Thread friction absorbs torque so the halves are clamped less, and the clearance reading is wrong.
mistakes.prevent: Clean the threads in the block and on the bolts and oil them lightly as specified.

mistakes.title: Oil behind the main shells
mistakes.what: Assembling the check with oil on the shell backs or in the bores.
mistakes.consequence: The shells do not seat fully, so the reading is off and heat transfer suffers.
mistakes.prevent: Keep shell backs and housing bores clean and dry; oil only the running face.

mistakes.title: Crank turned during the check
mistakes.what: Rotating the crankshaft with the Plastigage clamped in place.
mistakes.consequence: Every main bearing strip smears and the whole clamp-up has to be repeated with new strips.
mistakes.prevent: Keep the crank still until the halves are split again.

mistakes.title: Bearing ID measured at the split
mistakes.what: Measuring assembled bearing bore size close to the parting line.
mistakes.consequence: Shells are thinner toward the split by design, so the reading overstates clearance.
mistakes.prevent: Measure at 90 degrees to the parting line.

steps.title: Inspect pump, thermostat and pulleys
steps.action: Spin the water pump bearing, check the impeller, test the thermostat in heated water, and check the crank pulley, chain cover and pans for cracks.

mistakes.title: Old water pump reused
mistakes.what: Refitting the original water pump on a high-mileage engine because it spins freely.
mistakes.consequence: The seal weeps or the bearing fails soon after the rebuild, and coolant loss leads to overheating.
mistakes.prevent: Look for weep marks at the pump vent and bearing play, and replace a doubtful pump now.

mistakes.title: Thermostat not tested
mistakes.what: Refitting the thermostat without checking it opens in heated water.
mistakes.consequence: A sticking thermostat overheats the fresh engine during its first runs.
mistakes.prevent: Test it in heated water as the procedure describes, or fit a new one.

mistakes.title: Pump in chain cover not inspected
mistakes.what: Reusing the chain cover without looking at its built-in oil pump for debris marks.
mistakes.consequence: A scored pump gives low oil pressure, and the pump is not serviceable separately.
mistakes.prevent: Inspect the pump rotors and housing; if contamination has marked them, replace the chain cover.
mistakes.detect: Scoring on the rotors or housing, or low oil pressure at first start.

steps.title: Decide on head resurfacing
steps.action: Have any head beyond the warpage limit surfaced, but only while it stays at or above the minimum height; otherwise replace it.

spec.note: minimum head height after grinding (98.5 mm standard)

mistakes.title: Head ground below minimum
mistakes.what: Resurfacing a head past the minimum height.
mistakes.consequence: Combustion chamber volume and chain geometry change, and the head may not seal or time correctly.
mistakes.prevent: Confirm the head will stay at or above the minimum height before cutting; replace it otherwise.

mistakes.title: Machining chips left in the head
mistakes.what: Refitting a head straight from the machine shop without washing it.
mistakes.consequence: Chips in the oil lines reach the cam journals and AVCS sprockets.
mistakes.prevent: Wash every machined part and blow through each oil line before assembly.

steps.title: Replace worn valve guides
steps.action: Drive out worn guides from the combustion side, drive new oiled guides in from the cam side to the marked depth, ream them to size and clean out every chip.
steps.why: Guides go in before seat work because the seat cutter pilots off the guide bore.

mistakes.title: Guide protrusion out of spec
mistakes.what: Driving a new guide in without checking its protrusion.
mistakes.consequence: The stem seal and spring seat do not sit correctly on a guide at the wrong height.
mistakes.prevent: Drive to the marked depth and measure protrusion before reaming.

mistakes.title: Guide driven in dry or wrong way
mistakes.what: Installing guides unoiled or from the combustion side.
mistakes.consequence: The bore in the head galls and the guide is loose or cocked, ruining the head.
mistakes.prevent: Oil each new guide and drive it in from the cam side.

mistakes.title: Reaming chips left in guides
mistakes.what: Skipping the cleanup after reaming.
mistakes.consequence: Chips score the new valve stems and guides in the first minutes of running.
mistakes.prevent: Brush and wash each guide bore after reaming and before seat work.

steps.title: Cut and lap valve seats
steps.action: Cut each seat at 45 degrees, move the contact band with the 30 and 75 degree cutters until it is centered and in width, then lap each valve lightly and clean off all compound.
steps.why: Any replaced valve or reworked seat must be lapped so the dye check shows a continuous band.
steps.mistake: Leaving lapping compound in a guide or port wears the new guide in minutes.

mistakes.title: Lapping compound left in guide
mistakes.what: Not cleaning lapping compound out of the guide and port after lapping.
mistakes.consequence: The abrasive wears the new guide and stem within minutes of running.
mistakes.prevent: Wash the head, guides and ports thoroughly after lapping and before assembly.

mistakes.title: Seats cut before guides
mistakes.what: Cutting seats and then replacing guides.
mistakes.consequence: The seat is no longer concentric with the new guide and the valve will not seal.
mistakes.prevent: Replace guides first; the seat cutter pilots off the guide.

mistakes.title: Seat cut too deep
mistakes.what: Removing too much seat material while chasing a centered band.
mistakes.consequence: The valve sits deeper, which reduces cam clearance and may need a shim outside the available range.
mistakes.prevent: Cut in small passes and recheck band position and width often.

steps.title: Bore and hone to oversize
steps.action: If any bore is out of size, taper or round, or scored, bore and hone all four liners together for 0.25 or 0.50 mm oversize pistons, measuring only after the block cools to room temperature.
steps.why: Subaru requires all four bores to be done together so all pistons stay matched.
steps.mistake: Measuring right after honing reads small because the block is still warm.

mistakes.title: Bores measured while still warm
mistakes.what: Measuring bore size right after honing, before the block cools.
mistakes.consequence: The reading is false, so the bore ends up off size once the block reaches room temperature.
mistakes.prevent: Let the block cool to room temperature before the final measurement.

mistakes.title: Only damaged bores machined
mistakes.what: Boring or honing one cylinder and leaving the others.
mistakes.consequence: Subaru requires all four bores done together, and mixed piston sizes upset the matched set.
mistakes.prevent: Bore and hone all four cylinders together to the same oversize, as Subaru requires.

mistakes.title: Bores not scrubbed after honing
mistakes.what: Wiping the bores with solvent but not scrubbing out the honing grit.
mistakes.consequence: Abrasive left in the crosshatch wears rings and liners quickly and brings back oil consumption.
mistakes.prevent: Scrub with hot soapy water and a brush until a clean white rag comes out clean, then oil the bores.
mistakes.detect: A white rag wiped on the bore shows gray residue.

mistakes.title: Bore taken past maximum
mistakes.what: Opening a bore beyond the maximum diameter after boring.
mistakes.consequence: No oversize piston can give the right clearance and the block is scrap.
mistakes.prevent: Measure before the last cut and stop if the maximum would be exceeded.

steps.title: Resurface the block decks
steps.action: Only if the decks are past the warpage limit, have them surfaced while staying within the minimum block height.

spec.note: minimum block height after grinding (205.0 mm standard)

mistakes.title: Deck cut below minimum height
mistakes.what: Surfacing a block deck past the minimum block height.
mistakes.consequence: Compression and head gasket sealing change and the block may be unusable.
mistakes.prevent: Only surface a deck past its warpage limit, and stop at the minimum height.

steps.title: Grind or replace crankshaft
steps.action: If journals or pins are out of size or shape, grind to the size that matches the 0.03, 0.05 or 0.25 mm undersize bearings, or replace the crank.

spec.note: pin grind limit; main journal limit 67.735 mm

mistakes.title: Bearings not matched to grind size
mistakes.what: Grinding the crank and fitting bearings ordered before the final size was known.
mistakes.consequence: Oil clearance ends up too tight or too loose and the bearing fails.
mistakes.prevent: Order the matching undersize bearings after the grind and confirm with measurement.

mistakes.title: Fillet radii wrong after grind
mistakes.what: Accepting a grind with oversized or undersized fillet radii.
mistakes.consequence: An oversized fillet lets the bearing edge ride on it; an undersized one weakens the crank at its highest stress point.
mistakes.prevent: Check fillet radii against the manufacturer specification after grinding.

mistakes.title: Oil holes not blended after grind
mistakes.what: Leaving sharp edges at the oil holes after grinding.
mistakes.consequence: Sharp edges left at the journal oil holes scrape the soft bearing lining as the crank turns.
mistakes.prevent: Make sure oil holes are chamfered and polished into the journal surface.

steps.title: Replace rod small-end bushings
steps.action: Where pin-to-bushing clearance is out, press out the bushing, press in a new oiled one, drill its two oil holes through the rod's holes and ream it to fit.

mistakes.title: Bushing oil holes not drilled
mistakes.what: Pressing in a new small-end bushing without drilling its oil holes through the rod holes.
mistakes.consequence: The pin runs without oil, scuffs and can seize, wrecking the piston and rod.
mistakes.prevent: Drill both oil holes through the rod holes and deburr before reaming.

mistakes.title: Bushing pressed in dry or cocked
mistakes.what: Pressing the bushing in unoiled or at an angle.
mistakes.consequence: The bushing distorts or loosens and can turn, closing off its oil holes.
mistakes.prevent: Oil the new bushing and press it in square.

steps.title: Order kit and one-time parts
steps.action: Order the gasket set, bearings, rings and pistons as needed, plus the parts the manual treats as one-time use: rod cap bolts, every O-ring, AVCS filter screens, oil separator cover, front and rear seals and valve stem seals.
steps.why: A typical aftermarket rebuild kit leaves out the oil pump and timing parts, so chains, guides or tensioners must be sourced separately if needed.

mistakes.title: Parts ordered for wrong FB25 version
mistakes.what: Ordering pistons, rings or a kit without checking the engine code and VIN.
mistakes.consequence: FB25 parts changed over the years, including the oil control ring update, so mismatched parts may not fit or meet spec.
mistakes.prevent: Order by VIN and engine code (FB25BA or FB25BC) and confirm the ring set is the updated design.

mistakes.title: One-time parts reused to save money
mistakes.what: Planning to reuse rod bolts, O-rings, AVCS screens, the PCV adapter or the oil separator cover.
mistakes.consequence: Each can fail in its own way: loose caps, oil leaks, blocked AVCS oil or crankcase leaks.
mistakes.prevent: Order every one-time part listed in the notes before assembly starts.

mistakes.title: Timing parts left off the order
mistakes.what: Assuming the rebuild kit includes chains, guides and tensioners.
mistakes.consequence: Kits leave these out, and worn guides get reused rather than wait for parts.
mistakes.prevent: Decide on chain parts after inspection and order them separately.

mistakes.title: Pistons ordered without bore grade
mistakes.what: Ordering standard pistons without the stamped A or B bore grade.
mistakes.consequence: Pistons of the wrong grade arrive and piston-to-wall clearance cannot be brought into range.
mistakes.prevent: Order pistons by the grade stamped on each bore, or by the oversize after machining.

steps.title: Install gallery and block plugs
steps.action: Degrease the threads, coat the plugs with liquid gasket and install the main gallery plugs and block plug in both halves, then fit the block plate to the LH half.

spec.note: main gallery plugs (block plug 16 N·m); ThreeBond 1105 on threads

mistakes.title: Gallery plug left out
mistakes.what: Forgetting to refit a main gallery plug or the block plug.
mistakes.consequence: Oil pressure escapes through the open hole on first start and the bearings are wiped.
mistakes.prevent: Count the plugs back in against the teardown list and check each hole with a light.
mistakes.detect: Oil pouring out on priming, or no pressure on the gauge.

mistakes.title: Plug threads not degreased
mistakes.what: Coating oily threads with sealant.
mistakes.consequence: The sealant does not cure and the plug weeps or backs out.
mistakes.prevent: Degrease the threads in the block and on the plug before sealing.

mistakes.title: Wrong sealant on plug threads
mistakes.what: Using thread tape or the flange sealant instead of the specified thread sealant.
mistakes.consequence: Tape shreds can break off into the gallery, and the wrong product may not seal.
mistakes.prevent: Use ThreeBond 1105 on the gallery plug threads as specified.

steps.title: Fit new oil separator cover
steps.action: Run a bead of liquid gasket on a new oil separator cover, fit it to the RH half within five minutes and tighten the bolts in sequence.

mistakes.title: Old oil separator cover reused
mistakes.what: Refitting the original oil separator cover.
mistakes.consequence: It is a one-time part and can leak crankcase gases or oil.
mistakes.prevent: Fit a new cover with a fresh bead.

mistakes.title: Sealant bead past its open time
mistakes.what: Laying the bead and fitting the cover after the five-minute window.
mistakes.consequence: The skinned sealant does not bond and the cover leaks.
mistakes.prevent: Have the cover and bolts ready before applying the bead, and redo the bead if time runs out.

steps.title: Fit water jacket spacers
steps.action: Set the water jacket spacers into the RH and LH halves.

mistakes.title: Water jacket spacers omitted
mistakes.what: Forgetting to put the water jacket spacers back, or swapping them between halves.
mistakes.consequence: Coolant flow around the liners changes from what the engine was designed for, altering liner temperatures.
mistakes.prevent: Fit each spacer to its own half before the halves are joined.

steps.title: Assemble pistons to rods
steps.action: Fit one circlip, set the piston on the rod with the front mark and rod direction matched for its side, slide in the oiled pin, fit the second circlip and turn both gaps away from the groove notch.
steps.why: RH pistons (1 and 3) and LH pistons (2 and 4) face their rods differently; the orientation is fixed once the rod is in the bore.
steps.mistake: A circlip left with its gap at the groove notch can walk out and let the pin score the bore.

mistakes.title: Circlip gap at the groove notch
mistakes.what: Leaving a circlip with its gap at the notch in the pin bore groove.
mistakes.consequence: The clip can walk out, letting the pin slide and score the cylinder wall.
mistakes.prevent: Turn each circlip so its gap sits away from the groove notch.

mistakes.title: Piston wrong way on the rod
mistakes.what: Assembling a piston to its rod with the front mark not matched to that bank.
mistakes.consequence: Once in the bore the piston faces the wrong way, so its offset and valve reliefs are on the wrong side.
mistakes.prevent: Check the front mark and rod direction against the RH (1, 3) or LH (2, 4) figure before fitting the pin.

mistakes.title: Rod reversed for its bank
mistakes.what: Fitting the diagonally split rod in the wrong direction for the bank.
mistakes.consequence: The cap and bearing do not sit correctly on the crank pin and the bearing fails.
mistakes.prevent: Lay each assembly next to the figure for its bank before fitting the circlip.

mistakes.title: Pin assembled dry
mistakes.what: Sliding the pin in without oil.
mistakes.consequence: The pin and bushing scuff in the first seconds of running.
mistakes.prevent: Oil the pin, pin bores and bushing before assembly.

steps.title: Install the piston rings
steps.action: Fit the oil ring expander, lower rail and upper rail by hand, then the second and top rings with a ring expander, marks facing up.
steps.why: Upside-down compression rings pump oil into the chamber, the same symptom behind Subaru's FB oil consumption bulletins.
steps.mistake: Installing the second ring upside down raises oil consumption.

mistakes.title: Second ring upside down
mistakes.what: Fitting the second compression ring with its mark facing down.
mistakes.consequence: An upside-down ring pumps oil into the chamber and raises oil consumption.
mistakes.prevent: Check every compression ring mark faces up before closing the expander.

mistakes.title: Top and second rings swapped
mistakes.what: Fitting the top ring in the second groove and the second in the top.
mistakes.consequence: The rings have different profiles, so blow-by and oil consumption rise.
mistakes.prevent: Identify each ring by its profile and marking before fitting.

mistakes.title: Rings spiraled on by hand
mistakes.what: Winding compression rings into their grooves by hand.
mistakes.consequence: The ring twists or overstretches and its coating is damaged, so it never seals properly.
mistakes.prevent: Use a ring expander and open the ring only enough to clear the piston.

mistakes.title: Oil ring expander ends overlapped
mistakes.what: Letting the ends of the expander overlap behind the rails.
mistakes.consequence: The oil ring loses its tension and oil consumption is high from the start.
mistakes.prevent: Check that the expander ends butt with their color marks visible before fitting the rails.

mistakes.title: Superseded ring set fitted
mistakes.what: Using an older oil control ring design on an engine covered by the ring update.
mistakes.consequence: Subaru changed the oil control ring treatment to address FB oil consumption, so an old-style set can bring that problem back.
mistakes.prevent: Confirm the rings are the current Subaru part or the kit maker's updated set.

steps.title: Seat oiled main bearings
steps.action: Install the oiled main bearings in both halves in their original or selected positions and fit new O-rings to the LH half.

mistakes.title: Oil on main shell backs
mistakes.what: Oiling the back of the bearing shells or the housing bores.
mistakes.consequence: The shells do not seat solidly and heat transfer is poor, which shortens bearing life.
mistakes.prevent: Fit shells with clean, dry backs and bores; oil only the running face.

mistakes.title: Upper and lower shells swapped
mistakes.what: Fitting the plain shell where the grooved, holed shell belongs.
mistakes.consequence: The oil feed is blocked and that main bearing starves and fails.
mistakes.prevent: Match each shell to its half and check the oil hole lines up with the feed hole.
mistakes.detect: Oil hole visible through the shell when looking down the feed passage.

mistakes.title: Locating lug not in its notch
mistakes.what: Setting a shell with its lug beside the notch instead of in it.
mistakes.consequence: The shell is pinched out of round and wipes the journal.
mistakes.prevent: Seat each lug in its notch and press the shell flush at both ends.

mistakes.title: Dirt trapped behind a shell
mistakes.what: Fitting shells into bores with grit or a burr behind them.
mistakes.consequence: A high spot forms on the bearing face and wears through.
mistakes.prevent: Wipe each bore clean with a lint-free cloth right before fitting the shell.

mistakes.title: Assembly oil spread with a brush
mistakes.what: Applying oil to bearings with a brush dipped in an open container.
mistakes.consequence: The brush carries grit from the container onto the bearing faces.
mistakes.prevent: Use a clean oil can or squeeze bottle.

steps.title: Lay crankshaft in LH half
steps.action: Oil the main journals and lower the crankshaft into the LH half.
steps.why: The crank must go in before the halves are joined; nothing else installs between them except the bearings.

mistakes.title: Crank dropped into the shells
mistakes.what: Lowering the crank at an angle so it knocks a shell out of place.
mistakes.consequence: A shell knocked out of its seat is pinched when the halves close and wipes the journal.
mistakes.prevent: Lower the crank squarely and check every shell is still seated.

mistakes.title: Journals left dusty
mistakes.what: Laying the crank in without wiping the journals.
mistakes.consequence: Dust on the journals is trapped in the new bearings and scores them on the first start.
mistakes.prevent: Wipe each journal, then oil it, just before the crank goes in.

steps.title: Apply block-half sealant bead
steps.action: Degrease both mating faces and run the specified liquid gasket bead on the RH half, thin across most of the face and thicker in the marked ranges, keeping it clear of oil passages and bearing bores.
steps.why: Sealant squeezed into an oil passage or bearing can block oil and seize the engine; the halves must be joined within five minutes.

spec.note: bead diameter on most of the face; 4 mm in ranges A and C, 3.2 mm in range B; ThreeBond 1217G

steps.mistake: A heavy bead near a bearing saddle squeezes into the oil feed and starves that bearing.

mistakes.title: Heavy bead near a bearing saddle
mistakes.what: Laying too much sealant close to a main bearing saddle or oil passage.
mistakes.consequence: The excess squeezes into the oil feed and starves that bearing.
mistakes.prevent: Keep the bead at its specified size and clear of oil passages and bearing bores.

mistakes.title: Block halves joined past open time
mistakes.what: Taking longer than five minutes between starting the bead and joining the halves.
mistakes.consequence: The sealant skins and the block seam leaks, which can only be fixed by a full teardown.
mistakes.prevent: Rehearse the join, have bolts and tools laid out, and restart the bead if time runs out.

mistakes.title: Mating faces not degreased
mistakes.what: Applying the bead to faces with oil or old sealant residue.
mistakes.consequence: The sealant does not bond and the seam weeps oil.
mistakes.prevent: Clean both faces with a degreaser just before laying the bead.

mistakes.title: Bead broken or thin in marked ranges
mistakes.what: Leaving gaps in the bead or skipping the thicker ranges the manual marks.
mistakes.consequence: Oil finds the gap in the bead and seeps along the block seam, which needs a full teardown to fix.
mistakes.prevent: Lay one continuous bead, thicker in the marked ranges, and check it before joining.

steps.title: Join the block halves
steps.action: Set the RH half onto the LH half, lightly oil the joining bolt threads and washers, fit the bolts, and screw in two head bolts where shown to anchor the angle gauge.
steps.why: Only a light coat of oil goes on the bolts so none reaches the water jacket.

mistakes.title: RH half slid across the LH
mistakes.what: Setting the RH half down off position and sliding it into place.
mistakes.consequence: Sealant is smeared toward the bearing bores and oil passages and the bead is broken.
mistakes.prevent: Lower the RH half straight onto its dowels in one movement.

mistakes.title: Joining bolts over-oiled
mistakes.what: Dipping the joining bolts in oil instead of a light coat.
mistakes.consequence: Excess oil is carried into the water jacket and contaminates the coolant.
mistakes.prevent: Coat only the threads and washer faces lightly.

steps.title: Torque joining bolts first pass
steps.action: Holding only the LH half, tighten all joining bolts in the tightening sequence, back them all off 180 degrees in the loosening sequence, then tighten them all again.
steps.why: Seating, releasing and reseating the bolts draws the halves together evenly before any angle is added.

spec.note: all bolts, twice, with a 180 deg back-off between

steps.mistake: Holding the RH half while torquing pulls the halves out of alignment.

mistakes.title: RH half held while torquing
mistakes.what: Steadying the RH block half by hand while tightening the joining bolts.
mistakes.consequence: The halves are pulled out of alignment as the bolts draw down.
mistakes.prevent: Hold only the LH half while torquing, as the procedure specifies.

mistakes.title: Back-off step skipped
mistakes.what: Going straight from the first torque to the angle without the 180 degree release and retorque.
mistakes.consequence: The halves are not drawn together evenly and main clearance and sealing suffer.
mistakes.prevent: Follow the tighten, release and retighten cycle in the factory sequences.

mistakes.title: Torque wrench set in wrong units
mistakes.what: Setting the wrench in ft·lb when the spec is in N·m.
mistakes.consequence: The bolts are overloaded by a large margin and the aluminum threads can pull.
mistakes.prevent: Check the unit on the wrench scale before every new spec.

steps.title: Angle-torque the joining bolts
steps.action: Back off the first group of four bolts 180 degrees, tighten them to the lower torque and add the angle in sequence, then do the same for the group of six.

spec.note: after 17 N·m; four bolts first, then six

mistakes.title: Angle groups done out of order
mistakes.what: Angling the six-bolt group first or mixing bolts between groups.
mistakes.consequence: Clamp load builds unevenly across the case and the main bearing bores distort.
mistakes.prevent: Do the group of four first, then the group of six, each in sequence.

mistakes.title: Angle judged by eye
mistakes.what: Estimating the angle instead of using a gauge.
mistakes.consequence: Bolts end up under or over the angle range, changing clamp load.
mistakes.prevent: Use the angle gauge anchored to the temporary head bolts and paint-mark each bolt as it is done.

mistakes.title: Crank not turned after final torque
mistakes.what: Moving on without turning the crank by hand once the halves are torqued.
mistakes.consequence: A tight bearing or sealant in a bore goes unnoticed until the engine seizes.
mistakes.prevent: Turn the crank a full turn by hand after torquing; it should turn smoothly without tight spots.
mistakes.detect: Rotating torque that rises sharply or a tight spot each turn.

steps.title: Fit the outer joining bolt
steps.action: Remove the temporary head bolts, install the separate outer joining bolt and wipe any squeeze-out off the chain cover and oil pan faces, leaving sealant on the chamfers.

mistakes.title: Squeeze-out left on cover faces
mistakes.what: Leaving cured sealant squeeze-out on the chain cover and oil pan faces.
mistakes.consequence: The ridge holds those covers off the block and they leak later.
mistakes.prevent: Wipe the cover and pan faces clean while the sealant is still wet.

mistakes.title: Sealant wiped out of chamfers
mistakes.what: Cleaning the chamfers at the seam along with the faces.
mistakes.consequence: The corner where the block seam meets the chain cover and pan joints is left without sealant and leaks.
mistakes.prevent: Leave the sealant in the chamfers as the procedure specifies.

steps.title: Install the rear main seal
steps.action: Oil the new rear seal inside and out and press it on with the seal guide and installer.

mistakes.title: Rear seal fitted without guide
mistakes.what: Pushing the rear seal over the crank flange without the seal guide.
mistakes.consequence: The lip rolls or tears on the flange and the seal leaks into the bellhousing, so the engine comes out again.
mistakes.prevent: Slide the seal on over the factory seal guide, then press it home with the installer.

mistakes.title: Rear seal lip installed dry
mistakes.what: Fitting the seal without oiling it inside and out.
mistakes.consequence: The dry lip is burned on first start and leaks.
mistakes.prevent: Oil the seal inside and out before pressing it on.

mistakes.title: Rear seal cocked
mistakes.what: Pressing the seal in unevenly.
mistakes.consequence: A seal pressed in at an angle runs off-center on the crank flange and leaks oil.
mistakes.prevent: Press it in square with the installer until it is flush all round.

steps.title: Set the ring gap positions
steps.action: Stand the block rear down on the four bolts, then clock each top ring gap to its mark, the second ring opposite, the upper rail with its stopper in the side hole, the expander opposite the rail and the lower rail a further third of a turn round.
steps.why: Staggered gaps limit blow-by, and no gap may sit in line with the piston skirt.

spec.value: second ring 180 from top ring; expander 180 from upper rail; lower rail 120 clockwise from upper rail
spec.note: top ring and upper rail start at the positions in the factory figure

mistakes.title: Ring gaps lined up
mistakes.what: Leaving ring gaps in line with each other.
mistakes.consequence: Compression and oil pass straight through the lined-up gaps, raising blow-by and oil consumption.
mistakes.prevent: Clock each ring to its own position and recheck before the piston goes in.

mistakes.title: Generic ring clocking used
mistakes.what: Following a ring maker's general clocking diagram instead of the FB figure.
mistakes.consequence: Gaps can end up in line with the skirt or the rail stopper, which the FB layout avoids.
mistakes.prevent: Use the factory ring gap figure for this engine.

mistakes.title: Rail stopper not in its hole
mistakes.what: Fitting the upper oil rail without its stopper in the piston side hole.
mistakes.consequence: The rail is not held in position, so its gap can move to the wrong place.
mistakes.prevent: Seat the stopper in the side hole and check it before clocking the expander.

mistakes.title: Rings rotated by the compressor
mistakes.what: Clocking the gaps, then fitting the compressor with a twisting motion.
mistakes.consequence: The gaps move out of position before the piston goes in.
mistakes.prevent: Recheck the gap positions after the compressor is on.

steps.title: Install piston number one
steps.action: Oil the bore, piston and crank pin, bring the number 1 pin to top dead center, compress the rings and tap the piston in by its crown with the front mark forward.
steps.why: With the pin at the top, the rod can be steered onto it without hitting the liner.
steps.mistake: Letting the rod's big end strike the crank pin or liner on the way in nicks both.

mistakes.title: Big end strikes pin or liner
mistakes.what: Letting the rod big end hit the crank pin or the liner as the piston goes in.
mistakes.consequence: The crank pin and the liner are both nicked, and a nicked pin then cuts the new bearing.
mistakes.prevent: Bring the pin to top dead center and steer the rod onto it by hand from below.

mistakes.title: Compressor not flat on the deck
mistakes.what: Tapping the piston in with the ring compressor lifted off the deck on one side.
mistakes.consequence: A ring springs out between the compressor and deck and breaks.
mistakes.prevent: Hold the compressor flat against the deck while tapping.

mistakes.title: Piston hammered past resistance
mistakes.what: Hitting harder when the piston stops going in.
mistakes.consequence: A ring caught on the deck edge snaps or cracks the ring land under it.
mistakes.prevent: Stop as soon as it stops, release the compressor and find the caught ring.

mistakes.title: Front mark facing rearward
mistakes.what: Installing the piston with its front mark pointing to the rear of the engine.
mistakes.consequence: The piston and rod sit backward in the bore with offsets and reliefs on the wrong side.
mistakes.prevent: Check the front mark before each piston goes in.

mistakes.title: Bore oiled with dirty oil
mistakes.what: Oiling the bore and rings from an open, dusty container.
mistakes.consequence: Grit from the open container goes straight into the ring pack and liner.
mistakes.prevent: Oil the bore and rings from a clean, sealed bottle kept covered on the bench.

steps.title: Cap rod one, snug bolts
steps.action: Holding the piston down, turn the crank so the pin meets the big end, fit the matching cap with a new oiled bolt and tighten in two steps.
steps.why: Each cap only fits its own rod; the final angle comes later once all four are in.

spec.note: new bolt, oiled threads and seat

mistakes.title: Rod cap fitted reversed
mistakes.what: Fitting a rod cap backward on its rod.
mistakes.consequence: The cap does not match the rod, the bearing shell is misaligned, and the bearing spins.
mistakes.prevent: Match the cap marks to the rod and check that it sits flush with no step.

mistakes.title: Cap shell slips fitting from below
mistakes.what: Fitting the cap blind through the bottom of the block so its shell slides out of the notch.
mistakes.consequence: The shell is pinched and the bearing fails soon after start-up.
mistakes.prevent: Check the shell lug is in its notch just before offering the cap, and look again with a mirror if possible.

mistakes.title: Rod bolt threads not oiled
mistakes.what: Fitting the new rod bolts dry.
mistakes.consequence: More torque goes into friction, so the cap is clamped less than designed.
mistakes.prevent: Oil the threads and seat of each new bolt as specified.

mistakes.title: Oversize socket crowds the cap
mistakes.what: Using a thick-walled socket that presses against the cap as it tightens.
mistakes.consequence: The cap shifts sideways and the bearing wears at the parting lines.
mistakes.prevent: Use the specified rod bolt socket, which clears the cap.

steps.title: Install pistons two through four
steps.action: Repeat for pistons 2, 3 and 4, turning the crank clockwise to bring each pin to the top and fitting each cap to the same two-step torque.

mistakes.title: Piston in the wrong bank
mistakes.what: Fitting an RH piston and rod assembly into an LH bore.
mistakes.consequence: The piston and rod face the wrong way for that bank.
mistakes.prevent: Fit each assembly into its numbered bore: 1 and 3 RH, 2 and 4 LH.

mistakes.title: Crank turned with a rod unhooked
mistakes.what: Turning the crank to bring the next pin up while an earlier rod is not yet capped.
mistakes.consequence: The loose rod swings into the crank pin or liner and nicks it.
mistakes.prevent: Cap and snug each rod before turning to the next.

steps.title: Final-angle the rod bolts
steps.action: Thread cam carrier bolts into the block as anchors for the angle gauge, then add the final angle to the 1 and 4 cap bolts, rotate the crank and do the 2 and 3 cap bolts.
steps.why: Rod bolts are stretch-type and one-time use; the angle sets clamp load, not the torque reading.
steps.mistake: Reusing old rod bolts or skipping the angle lets a cap loosen and spin a bearing.

mistakes.title: Old rod bolts or no angle
mistakes.what: Reusing the old rod bolts or stopping at the snug torque without the final angle.
mistakes.consequence: Clamp load is too low, a cap can loosen, and the bearing spins.
mistakes.prevent: Use new rod bolts every time and complete the final angle on all eight.

mistakes.title: Angle gauge anchor slips
mistakes.what: Bracing the angle gauge arm against something that moves.
mistakes.consequence: The gauge reads more angle than the bolt actually turned, leaving it under-tightened.
mistakes.prevent: Anchor the gauge to the cam carrier bolts threaded into the block as the procedure shows.

mistakes.title: Rod bolt missed after rotating
mistakes.what: Losing track of which bolts got the final angle when the crank is rotated between pairs.
mistakes.consequence: A bolt left at the snug torque lets that cap loosen and the bearing spin.
mistakes.prevent: Paint-mark each bolt head as soon as it is angled.
mistakes.detect: An unmarked bolt head when checking all eight.

mistakes.title: Stop-start pull on the angle
mistakes.what: Turning the bolt through the angle in several jerky pulls.
mistakes.consequence: Friction changes each time the bolt stops, so clamp load scatters between bolts.
mistakes.prevent: Pull through the angle in one smooth motion.

steps.title: Assemble lower pan and strainer
steps.action: Fit the strainer with a new O-ring and the baffle plate to the oil pan upper, then bond the lower pan to it with a liquid gasket bead and a new seal ring.

mistakes.title: Pickup O-ring reused or pinched
mistakes.what: Fitting the strainer with its old O-ring or rolling the new one as it goes in.
mistakes.consequence: The pump draws air at the joint, giving low or fluctuating oil pressure.
mistakes.prevent: Fit a new oiled O-ring and seat the strainer straight before tightening.

mistakes.title: Strainer screen not cleaned
mistakes.what: Refitting the strainer without cleaning its screen.
mistakes.consequence: Debris from the old engine restricts flow to the pump.
mistakes.prevent: Clean and inspect the strainer and screen before fitting.

mistakes.title: Sealant squeezed into the pan
mistakes.what: Running a heavy bead on the lower pan so sealant squeezes inside.
mistakes.consequence: Strings of cured sealant break off and block the pickup screen.
mistakes.prevent: Use the specified bead size and check the inside of the joint after fitting.

mistakes.title: Baffle plate left out
mistakes.what: Forgetting the baffle plate when the strainer goes on.
mistakes.consequence: Oil sloshes away from the pickup in hard cornering and braking.
mistakes.prevent: Fit the baffle plate with the strainer as the procedure lists.

steps.title: Install oil pan upper
steps.action: Turn the block oil pan up, remove the four foot bolts, run a bead on the oil pan upper just outside the chamfer, fit a new O-ring and tighten the bolts in sequence.
steps.mistake: Getting sealant on the O-ring at the oil passage stops it sealing.

mistakes.title: Sealant smeared on passage O-ring
mistakes.what: Letting the oil pan upper sealant bead touch the O-ring at the oil passage.
mistakes.consequence: The O-ring no longer seals and oil leaks at that passage.
mistakes.prevent: Keep the bead clear of the O-ring and fit the O-ring after laying the bead.

mistakes.title: Oil pan upper O-ring reused
mistakes.what: Refitting the old O-ring at the oil passage between pan and block.
mistakes.consequence: The O-ring is not reusable, and the joint leaks or loses oil pressure.
mistakes.prevent: Fit a new O-ring every time the oil pan upper comes off.

mistakes.title: Bead laid inside the chamfer
mistakes.what: Running the bead inside the chamfer instead of just outside it.
mistakes.consequence: Sealant squeezes into the crankcase and can reach the pickup.
mistakes.prevent: Lay the bead just outside the chamfer, where the procedure places it.

mistakes.title: Pan bolts tightened out of order
mistakes.what: Tightening the pan bolts at random.
mistakes.consequence: The pan pulls down unevenly and the known pan-to-block leak point weeps.
mistakes.prevent: Tighten the pan bolts in numerical order to the specified torque.

steps.title: Fit thermostat and water pump
steps.action: Install the thermostat and cover with a new gasket, and the water pump on the oil pan upper with a new gasket.

mistakes.title: Thermostat fitted wrong way round
mistakes.what: Installing the thermostat reversed or out of its seat.
mistakes.consequence: Coolant flow is restricted and the freshly built engine overheats on its first runs.
mistakes.prevent: Check the thermostat orientation and seat against the figure before fitting the cover.

mistakes.title: Small bolts stripped in the pan
mistakes.what: Overtightening the thermostat cover or water pump bolts into the aluminum pan.
mistakes.consequence: The small threads in the aluminum pan strip and the joint weeps coolant.
mistakes.prevent: Use an inch-pound or small N·m torque wrench for the low spec.

steps.title: Remount block on the stand
steps.action: Bolt the stand adapters back to the block and oil pan upper and remount the assembly on the stand.

mistakes.title: Stand adapter bolts left loose
mistakes.what: Remounting the block on the stand without torquing the adapter bolts.
mistakes.consequence: The engine shifts or drops as it is rotated during head and timing work.
mistakes.prevent: Torque the adapter bolts before rotating the engine.

steps.title: Fit crank sensor and drive plate
steps.action: Install the crank position sensor and holder on the LH half, then the drive plate with its sensor plate.

spec.note: crank position sensor; drive plate torque is in the CVT section (not sourced here)

mistakes.title: Sensor plate not indexed on dowel
mistakes.what: Bolting the drive plate and crank sensor plate on without seating the sensor plate on its dowel pin.
mistakes.consequence: The crank signal is out of time and the engine will not start, and fixing it means pulling the engine again.
mistakes.prevent: Line up the hole in the sensor plate with the dowel in the crank flange and check it before tightening.
mistakes.detect: A crank-cam correlation code or no-start with good spark hardware.

mistakes.title: Crank sensor tip contaminated
mistakes.what: Fitting the crank sensor with metal particles stuck to its tip.
mistakes.consequence: The signal is weak or noisy and the engine misfires or sets crank sensor codes.
mistakes.prevent: Clean the sensor tip and check the sensor plate teeth before fitting.

steps.title: Install the PCV valve
steps.action: Coat the PCV valve threads with liquid gasket, install it in the RH half and refit its hose.

mistakes.title: Old PCV valve reused unchecked
mistakes.what: Refitting the original PCV valve without testing it.
mistakes.consequence: A sticking valve pressurizes the crankcase or pulls oil into the intake, causing leaks and oil consumption.
mistakes.prevent: Test or replace the PCV valve, and look for oil residue in the intake that points to a fault.

mistakes.title: Sealant blocks the PCV valve
mistakes.what: Using too much thread sealant so it enters the valve.
mistakes.consequence: Sealant inside the valve sticks it, and crankcase ventilation stops working.
mistakes.prevent: Apply a thin coat of ThreeBond 1141G to the threads only.

steps.title: Install the knock sensor
steps.action: Bolt the knock sensor to the LH half with its connector angled toward the front of the engine within the specified window.

spec.note: connector center 76.5 to 91.5 deg toward the front

mistakes.title: Knock sensor torque off
mistakes.what: Tightening the knock sensor by feel.
mistakes.consequence: Too loose or too tight changes how well it picks up knock, so the engine can knock without timing retard or set sensor codes.
mistakes.prevent: Torque it to spec on a clean mounting face.

mistakes.title: Connector angle outside the window
mistakes.what: Fitting the sensor with its connector pointing outside the specified angle.
mistakes.consequence: The harness is strained or cannot reach, and the connector can crack.
mistakes.prevent: Set the connector angle to the specified window before torquing.

steps.title: Fit water pipe and hanger
steps.action: Fit new O-rings, install the water pipe and PCV connector set, then the rear engine hanger.

spec.note: rear hanger; water pipe bolts 6.4 N·m

mistakes.title: Water pipe O-rings pinched
mistakes.what: Pushing the water pipe and PCV connector set in with dry or misplaced O-rings.
mistakes.consequence: A pinched O-ring leaks coolant at the pipe or lets crankcase air past the PCV connector.
mistakes.prevent: Lubricate new O-rings and push the pipe in straight before bolting it.

steps.title: Slide on the crank sprocket
steps.action: Slide the crank sprocket onto the crank key; either face can go outward.
steps.why: It must be on before the heads so the chains can be hung later without disturbing them.

mistakes.title: Crank key not seated
mistakes.what: Sliding the crank sprocket on with the key missing or riding out of its slot.
mistakes.consequence: The sprocket can slip on the crank, losing timing on both banks and letting valves hit pistons.
mistakes.prevent: Seat the key fully and check the sprocket slides on with no play.

steps.title: Press in valve stem seals
steps.action: Oil each new stem seal and press it onto its guide by hand with the seal guide tool, gray seals on intake and green on exhaust.
steps.why: Driving the tool with a hammer distorts the seal lip.
steps.mistake: Swapping the gray intake and green exhaust seals changes oil control at the guides.

mistakes.title: Gray and green stem seals swapped
mistakes.what: Fitting the exhaust (green) seals on intake guides and the intake (gray) seals on exhaust guides.
mistakes.consequence: Oil metering at the guides is wrong, which shows up as smoke or oil use.
mistakes.prevent: Sort the seals by color before starting: gray on intake, green on exhaust.

mistakes.title: Stem seals hammered into place
mistakes.what: Driving the seal installer with a hammer.
mistakes.consequence: The seal lip distorts and leaks oil down the valve stem.
mistakes.prevent: Press each seal on by hand with the seal guide tool.

mistakes.title: Seal lip cut by stem grooves
mistakes.what: Sliding the valve through a fitted seal without protecting the lip from the collet grooves.
mistakes.consequence: The sharp grooves nick the lip and the seal leaks from the first start.
mistakes.prevent: Oil the stem and cover the collet grooves with a thin sleeve or tape as the valve passes through.

steps.title: Reassemble valves and springs
steps.action: Set the spring seat, spring (close coils down) and retainer, slide in the oiled valve, compress the spring and fit the collets, then tap each retainer to seat them.

mistakes.title: Collets not fully seated
mistakes.what: Releasing the spring compressor without checking both collets are in the groove.
mistakes.consequence: A collet can pop out at speed and the valve drops into the cylinder.
mistakes.prevent: Tap each retainer after assembly and check both collet halves sit evenly.
mistakes.detect: One collet half standing proud of the other.

mistakes.title: Spring fitted upside down
mistakes.what: Installing a valve spring with its close-wound coils away from the head.
mistakes.consequence: The spring does not control the valve as designed at high rpm.
mistakes.prevent: Fit every spring with the close coils down against the spring seat.

mistakes.title: Spring seat left out
mistakes.what: Assembling a valve without its spring seat.
mistakes.consequence: The spring wears into the aluminum head and installed height is wrong.
mistakes.prevent: Lay out seat, spring, retainer and collets for each valve before compressing.

mistakes.title: Valve in the wrong guide
mistakes.what: Fitting a lapped valve into a different guide and seat.
mistakes.consequence: The valve and seat do not match and the cylinder leaks compression.
mistakes.prevent: Install each valve in the position it was lapped to.

steps.title: Refit head studs
steps.action: Install the stud bolts in both heads and the chain cover bolt in the LH head.

spec.note: two stud sizes; chain cover bolt 6.4 N·m

mistakes.title: Stud sizes put in wrong holes
mistakes.what: Mixing the two stud sizes or torques between holes.
mistakes.consequence: Overtightening the small studs strips the aluminum threads in the head.
mistakes.prevent: Match each stud to its hole and use the torque for its size.

steps.title: Clean head bolt holes
steps.action: Blow every head bolt hole in the block clean and dry with compressed air.
steps.why: Coolant or oil left in a blind hole gives a false torque reading and can crack the block.

mistakes.title: Fluid left in a blind bolt hole
mistakes.what: Leaving oil, coolant or solvent in a head bolt hole.
mistakes.consequence: The bolt hydraulically locks on the fluid, giving a false torque and possibly cracking the block.
mistakes.prevent: Blow every hole dry with compressed air and check with a light.

mistakes.title: Head bolt threads not chased
mistakes.what: Fitting head bolts into block threads still holding old sealant or corrosion.
mistakes.consequence: Thread friction absorbs torque, clamp load is low and the head gasket can leak.
mistakes.prevent: Clean all block threads with a thread chaser before the final blow-out.

mistakes.title: Cutting tap used on threads
mistakes.what: Running a cutting tap instead of a chaser through the head bolt holes.
mistakes.consequence: Metal is removed from the threads, which can then pull out under head bolt load.
mistakes.prevent: Use thread chasers, which clean threads without cutting them.

steps.title: Seal and place RH gasket
steps.action: Degrease the faces, put the specified liquid gasket bead on both sides of a new RH head gasket where marked and place it so the sealant squeezes out at the edge.
steps.why: The head must go on within five minutes of applying sealant.

mistakes.title: L and R head gaskets swapped
mistakes.what: Fitting the head gasket marked for the other bank.
mistakes.consequence: Coolant and oil holes do not line up, causing overheating or leaks.
mistakes.prevent: Check the L or R marking on each gasket before applying sealant.

mistakes.title: Gasket sealant in the wrong places
mistakes.what: Applying sealant away from the marked areas or too much of it.
mistakes.consequence: Excess sealant squeezes into a cylinder or blocks part of a coolant passage.
mistakes.prevent: Apply only the specified bead size at the marked positions.

mistakes.title: Faces not degreased before sealant
mistakes.what: Applying gasket sealant to head and deck faces that still have oil on them.
mistakes.consequence: The sealant does not stick and the gasket edge seeps oil or coolant.
mistakes.prevent: Wipe both faces with degreaser right before applying the beads.

mistakes.title: Head fitted after open time
mistakes.what: Taking longer than five minutes between sealing the gasket and setting the head.
mistakes.consequence: The skinned sealant cannot bond to the head, and the gasket edge seeps.
mistakes.prevent: Have the head, bolts and wrench ready before the sealant goes on.

steps.title: Snug the RH head bolts
steps.action: Oil the head bolt threads and washers, set the RH head, tighten all bolts in sequence to the first torque, then to the second.
steps.mistake: If a bolt creaks with stick-slip while tightening, the whole procedure has to be restarted with fresh sealant.

mistakes.title: Head bolt creaks during tightening
mistakes.what: Carrying on after a bolt makes a stick-slip creak while being tightened.
mistakes.consequence: That bolt has not reached its correct clamp load, and the procedure cannot be finished properly from there.
mistakes.prevent: Stop and restart the whole procedure with fresh sealant if any bolt creaks.

mistakes.title: Head bolts fitted dry
mistakes.what: Installing head bolts without oil on the threads and washers.
mistakes.consequence: Friction is higher than the procedure assumes, so the head is clamped less.
mistakes.prevent: Clean the bolt threads and coat threads and washers with engine oil.

mistakes.title: Damaged head bolts reused
mistakes.what: Reusing head bolts with stretched, necked or damaged threads.
mistakes.consequence: A weakened bolt cannot hold its clamp load and the gasket can leak.
mistakes.prevent: Inspect every bolt for necking and thread damage and replace any doubtful ones (many builders replace all).

mistakes.title: Moly or stud lube on factory bolts
mistakes.what: Using a low-friction assembly lube instead of engine oil on the factory bolts.
mistakes.consequence: With less friction the factory torque and angle overstretch the bolts and overload the threads.
mistakes.prevent: Use plain engine oil, which the factory procedure is based on.

steps.title: Release and retorque RH bolts
steps.action: Back every bolt off 180 degrees in the loosening sequence, then another 180 degrees, then tighten all in the tightening sequence to the working torque.
steps.why: Seating the gasket at high torque and then releasing it removes friction before the final stretch.

mistakes.title: Release steps done in wrong order
mistakes.what: Backing off the head bolts in the tightening order or skipping the second 180 degree release.
mistakes.consequence: The gasket is not relaxed evenly, so the final clamp load varies from bolt to bolt.
mistakes.prevent: Release in the loosening sequence, twice, before retorquing.

mistakes.title: Angle added without the retorque
mistakes.what: Adding the angle passes straight after the release without the working torque step.
mistakes.consequence: Bolts start their stretch from different points and end up under or over clamped.
mistakes.prevent: Bring every bolt to the working torque in sequence before any angle.

steps.title: Angle-torque the RH head
steps.action: Add the first angle to all bolts in order, then the second angle to the two named bolts, then the third angle to the four named bolts, and wipe any sealant off the chain cover face.

spec.note: all bolts; then +75 deg on 2 bolts; then +30 deg on 4 bolts

steps.mistake: Applying the 75 and 30 degree passes to the wrong bolts overloads some and underloads others.

mistakes.title: Extra angles on wrong bolts
mistakes.what: Applying the 75 and 30 degree passes to bolts other than the ones the procedure names.
mistakes.consequence: Some head bolts are overloaded while others are left under-clamped, so the gasket can leak.
mistakes.prevent: Mark the two and the four named bolts with paint before starting the angle passes.

mistakes.title: Squeeze-out left on cover face
mistakes.what: Leaving gasket sealant squeeze-out on the head's chain cover face.
mistakes.consequence: The cured ridge holds the chain cover off and it leaks.
mistakes.prevent: Wipe the chain cover face clean while the sealant is wet.

mistakes.title: Angle passes out of sequence
mistakes.what: Doing the angle passes in a random bolt order.
mistakes.consequence: The head is pulled down unevenly across its face and can distort.
mistakes.prevent: Follow the numerical bolt order for every one of the angle passes.

steps.title: Install and torque LH head
steps.action: Seal a new LH gasket the same way and run the identical torque, release, retorque and three-stage angle procedure on the LH head in its own sequence.

spec.note: after 29, 100, 2 x 180 deg release and 42 N·m

mistakes.title: RH sequence used on LH head
mistakes.what: Copying the RH bolt order onto the LH head.
mistakes.consequence: The LH head is pulled down in the wrong pattern and may not seal.
mistakes.prevent: Use the LH figure for its own sequence and named bolts.

mistakes.title: LH sealant applied too early
mistakes.what: Sealing the LH gasket while still working on the RH head.
mistakes.consequence: The LH gasket sealant skins over before the head is set on it.
mistakes.prevent: Finish the RH procedure completely before sealing the LH gasket.

steps.title: Mount the A/C compressor
steps.action: Bolt the A/C compressor back onto its mounting on the LH side.
steps.why: The manual refits the compressor right after the LH head is torqued and before the LH cam carrier goes on.

mistakes.title: Compressor fitted out of order
mistakes.what: Leaving the A/C compressor until after the LH cam carrier is on.
mistakes.consequence: Its mounting bolts are harder to reach and the carrier may have to come off again.
mistakes.prevent: Bolt the compressor on right after the LH head is torqued.

steps.title: Install the EGR pipe
steps.action: Fit the EGR pipe to the water pipe and RH block half with a new gasket.

mistakes.title: EGR gasket reused
mistakes.what: Refitting the EGR pipe with its old gasket.
mistakes.consequence: The joint leaks exhaust, upsetting EGR flow and setting codes.
mistakes.prevent: Fit a new EGR pipe gasket, which Subaru lists as a replacement part.

steps.title: Fit new AVCS filter screens
steps.action: Press a new AVCS filter screen into each cam carrier flush with the end face, no deeper than 0.5 mm.
steps.why: The screens are one-time use and protect the oil supply to the AVCS sprockets.

mistakes.title: AVCS screen pressed too deep
mistakes.what: Driving the new screen further in than flush with the carrier face.
mistakes.consequence: The deformed screen restricts oil to the AVCS sprocket and causes slow-response codes.
mistakes.prevent: Press it flush, never more than 0.5 mm below the end face.

mistakes.title: AVCS screen rotated in its bore
mistakes.what: Installing the screen without lining up its side hole with the carrier oil passage.
mistakes.consequence: Oil to the AVCS is blocked or restricted, which can damage the engine.
mistakes.prevent: Line up the hole in the screen tube with the passage before pressing it in.

mistakes.title: Original screens left in carriers
mistakes.what: Leaving old screens in place when the carriers were stripped.
mistakes.consequence: Debris already trapped in the old screens stays in the AVCS oil feed.
mistakes.prevent: Fit new screens whenever the carriers are stripped for service.

steps.title: Assemble camshafts into carriers
steps.action: Oil the journals, lay the camshafts in each carrier, run thin sealant beads on the front and rear cap faces and torque the caps in sequence.
steps.why: Too much sealant here can flow onto a journal and seize the camshaft.

spec.note: cam cap bolts in numerical order

mistakes.title: Too much sealant on cam caps
mistakes.what: Running a thick sealant bead on the front and rear cam cap faces.
mistakes.consequence: Sealant flows onto a journal and can seize the camshaft.
mistakes.prevent: Lay a thin bead only where the procedure shows.

mistakes.title: Cam caps in wrong positions
mistakes.what: Fitting caps to positions or directions other than the ones they were machined in.
mistakes.consequence: The bore no longer lines up with the carrier, so the cam binds or seizes.
mistakes.prevent: Follow the cap markings and the layout made at teardown.

mistakes.title: Cap bolts torqued out of sequence
mistakes.what: Tightening the cam cap bolts at random.
mistakes.consequence: The cam is pulled down unevenly and can bend or bind.
mistakes.prevent: Torque the cam cap bolts in numerical order, in stages.

mistakes.title: Cam journals assembled dry
mistakes.what: Laying cams in without oiling the journals.
mistakes.consequence: Journals scuff on first start and the AVCS responds slowly.
mistakes.prevent: Oil every journal and lobe before fitting the caps.

mistakes.title: Cap-to-carrier O-rings reused
mistakes.what: Reusing the two O-rings between a cam cap and the carrier.
mistakes.consequence: The joint seeps oil, a common FB leak that needs a reseal.
mistakes.prevent: Fit new O-rings whenever a cap comes off.

steps.title: Set RH rocker gear
steps.action: Stand the engine RH cams up, oil and install each shim and pivot in its original place, then the oiled roller rockers and new O-rings.
steps.why: Each shim must go back on its own valve or every clearance changes.

mistakes.title: Carrier-to-head O-rings reused
mistakes.what: Refitting the cam carrier with the old O-rings between it and the head.
mistakes.consequence: Oil seeps between carrier and head, a known FB leak point.
mistakes.prevent: Fit new O-rings at every carrier-to-head joint before setting the carrier.

mistakes.title: Rocker not seated on valve
mistakes.what: Leaving a roller rocker sitting off its pivot or valve tip when the carrier goes on.
mistakes.consequence: As the carrier tightens, the rocker breaks or the valve bends.
mistakes.prevent: Check each rocker sits on its pivot and valve before lowering the carrier.

mistakes.title: Shim back on the wrong valve
mistakes.what: Fitting a shim from the tray to a valve other than its own.
mistakes.consequence: That valve and the one it came from both end up out of clearance.
mistakes.prevent: Work from the labeled tray one valve at a time.

steps.title: Torque the RH cam carrier
steps.action: Seal the carrier face, set both cams to zero lift, set the carrier and tighten all bolts in sequence, then three times back off the three named bolts 180 degrees and retighten them.
steps.why: Zero lift means no valve spring is pushing up while the carrier draws down.

spec.note: all bolts, then three release-and-retighten cycles on 3 bolts

steps.mistake: Setting the carrier with a lobe on a rocker can bend a valve or crack the carrier.

mistakes.title: Carrier set with a lobe loaded
mistakes.what: Setting the cam carrier while a lobe is on a rocker.
mistakes.consequence: Uneven spring load as the carrier draws down can bend a valve or crack the carrier.
mistakes.prevent: Put both cams at zero lift before the carrier touches the head.

mistakes.title: Carrier face not degreased
mistakes.what: Laying the carrier bead on an oily face.
mistakes.consequence: The bead does not bond and the carrier-to-head joint seeps oil after the rebuild.
mistakes.prevent: Degrease both faces just before laying the bead.

mistakes.title: Carrier release cycles skipped
mistakes.what: Skipping the three back-off and retighten cycles on the named bolts.
mistakes.consequence: The carrier does not seat evenly and the joint may leak.
mistakes.prevent: Do all three cycles on the three named bolts.

steps.title: Install the LH cam carrier
steps.action: Roll the engine LH cams up, fit the LH shims, pivots, rockers and O-rings, seal the carrier and torque it with the same zero-lift and three-cycle procedure.

mistakes.title: LH carrier set with lobe loaded
mistakes.what: Fitting the LH carrier without checking both LH cams are at zero lift.
mistakes.consequence: A loaded lobe pushes the carrier unevenly and can crack it or bend a valve.
mistakes.prevent: Turn both LH cams to zero lift and recheck just before setting the carrier.

mistakes.title: LH bead broken at cap corners
mistakes.what: Leaving gaps in the LH carrier bead around the cam cap corners.
mistakes.consequence: Oil leaks out at the corners where the cam cap and carrier meet.
mistakes.prevent: Run one unbroken bead around each cap corner before lowering the carrier.

steps.title: Bolt on the cam sprockets
steps.action: Fit each sprocket on its camshaft knock pin, hold it with the pulley wrench and pin set, and torque the bolts.

mistakes.title: Sprocket fitted to wrong cam
mistakes.what: Installing a sprocket on a camshaft it did not come from.
mistakes.consequence: AVCS function or timing is wrong and the chain cover has to come off.
mistakes.prevent: Match each sprocket to its tag before fitting.

mistakes.title: Sprocket off its knock pin
mistakes.what: Torquing a sprocket bolt with the sprocket not engaged on the cam knock pin.
mistakes.consequence: The sprocket sits cocked, the timing is off and oil can leak past.
mistakes.prevent: Check the pin is engaged and the sprocket sits flat before torquing.

steps.title: Measure cam clearance
steps.action: With each lobe on its base circle, measure between the cam and the roller with a feeler gauge and record every reading.
steps.why: Clearance is set by shim thickness, so it must be checked before chains and covers make the carriers hard to remove.
steps.mistake: Turning a cam past its free range to reach a lobe makes intake and exhaust valves collide.

mistakes.title: Cam turned past free range
mistakes.what: Rotating a cam beyond its free range to bring a lobe round for measuring.
mistakes.consequence: The intake and exhaust valves of that cylinder hit each other and bend.
mistakes.prevent: Measure only lobes reachable within the free range, then reposition safely.

mistakes.title: Clearance read off base circle
mistakes.what: Measuring while the lobe is partly lifted.
mistakes.consequence: The clearance reads tight and the wrong shim gets fitted.
mistakes.prevent: Measure only with the lobe pointing away from the roller.

mistakes.title: Clearance readings not recorded
mistakes.what: Measuring every valve but not writing the readings down.
mistakes.consequence: There is nothing to calculate new shims from, so every valve has to be remeasured.
mistakes.prevent: Record each reading against its valve on a sheet.

mistakes.title: Later engine clearance spec used
mistakes.what: Checking against a cam clearance from a different FB25 version.
mistakes.consequence: Valves are set tighter or looser than this engine needs, giving noise or burned valves.
mistakes.prevent: Use the clearance for the exact engine and check STIS by VIN.

steps.title: Correct clearance with new shims
steps.action: For any valve out of range, measure its shim, calculate the new thickness, fit a new shim, refit the carrier and recheck every valve on that side.

spec.note: intake; exhaust S = T + 1.69 x (V - 0.22); S new, T current shim, V measured

mistakes.title: Intake and exhaust constants mixed
mistakes.what: Calculating an exhaust shim with the intake formula constant, or the reverse.
mistakes.consequence: The calculated shim is the wrong thickness, so the clearance stays out of range.
mistakes.prevent: Use 1.54 for intake and 1.69 for exhaust on this engine.

mistakes.title: Later formula constants used
mistakes.what: Using the shim constants from the 2015 and later Legacy manual.
mistakes.consequence: The later engine has a different rocker ratio, so the calculated shim is wrong.
mistakes.prevent: Use the constants from the manual for this engine.

mistakes.title: Clearance not rechecked after shimming
mistakes.what: Fitting new shims and moving on without remeasuring.
mistakes.consequence: A misread gauge or a wrong shim goes into service unnoticed.
mistakes.prevent: Refit the carrier and recheck every valve on that side.

steps.title: Load the LH tensioner
steps.action: Push the LH tensioner plunger in with the link plate, make sure the first rack notch is engaged and lock it with the stopper pin.

mistakes.title: LH tensioner rack not engaged
mistakes.what: Pinning the LH plunger without the first rack notch engaged.
mistakes.consequence: The tensioner does not take up the chain correctly and the chain rattles.
mistakes.prevent: Confirm the first notch is engaged before inserting the pin.

mistakes.title: Stopper pin falls out
mistakes.what: Using a pin too short or thin to stay in the stopper hole.
mistakes.consequence: The plunger releases while the chain is being hung and has to be reset.
mistakes.prevent: Use a 2.5 mm pin long enough to stay in and check it is secure.

steps.title: Confirm crank parked mid-stroke
steps.action: Check the crank sprocket mark is still at the parked position with all pistons halfway down.
steps.why: The LH intake cam is turned next, and that is only safe with no piston near the top.

mistakes.title: Assumed crank still parked
mistakes.what: Skipping the check because the crank was parked during teardown.
mistakes.consequence: The crank may have moved during short block work and a piston is near an open valve.
mistakes.prevent: Check the sprocket mark against the parked position before touching the LH intake cam.

steps.title: Time the LH intake sprocket
steps.action: Turn the LH intake sprocket with the pulley wrench to its timing mark, without touching the LH exhaust cam.
steps.mistake: Nudging the LH exhaust cam while the intake is lifted lets the valves meet.

mistakes.title: LH exhaust nudged during intake timing
mistakes.what: Bumping the LH exhaust cam while the LH intake is lifting valves.
mistakes.consequence: The LH exhaust valves meet the lifted intake valves and bend.
mistakes.prevent: Keep tools and hands off the exhaust sprocket while turning the intake.

mistakes.title: LH intake timed to free plate
mistakes.what: Aligning the LH intake to its sensor plate mark when the plate was free.
mistakes.consequence: The LH intake ends up out of time and sets correlation codes.
mistakes.prevent: Use the housing mark on any sprocket tagged with a free plate.

steps.title: Roll crank back 200 degrees
steps.action: Turn the crank about 200 degrees counterclockwise to bring the key to its LH timing position, only going clockwise for the last fine adjustment.
steps.why: This is the teardown move in reverse; turning clockwise here would push pistons into the open LH intake valves.

mistakes.title: Crank rolled back clockwise
mistakes.what: Turning the crank clockwise to reach the LH timing position.
mistakes.consequence: Pistons rise into the LH intake valves that are being held open.
mistakes.prevent: Turn counterclockwise for the move and only clockwise for the final nudge.

mistakes.title: Keyway used as the crank mark
mistakes.what: Lining up the crank keyway instead of the sprocket timing mark.
mistakes.consequence: The crank is off position and both banks can end up out of time.
mistakes.prevent: Use the oval timing mark on the front of the sprocket, beside the keyway.

steps.title: Time the LH exhaust sprocket
steps.action: Set the LH exhaust sprocket to its mark, turning it only within its free zero-lift range.

mistakes.title: LH exhaust turned outside free range
mistakes.what: Turning the LH exhaust sprocket beyond the range where it moves freely.
mistakes.consequence: The exhaust valves meet the already open LH intake valves and bend.
mistakes.prevent: Move the LH exhaust sprocket only within its free zero-lift range.

steps.title: Hang the LH timing chain
steps.action: Fit the LH chain with its blue link on the crank sprocket mark and its two pink links on the LH intake and exhaust timing marks, then fit the LH guide.
steps.why: Use the housing marks on any sprocket whose sensor plate was found free.
steps.mistake: Counting links instead of matching the colored links is the usual way the LH bank ends up a tooth off.

mistakes.title: Counting links instead of colored links
mistakes.what: Timing the LH chain by counting links rather than matching its colored links.
mistakes.consequence: The LH bank ends up one tooth off, which shows as correlation codes.
mistakes.prevent: Match the blue link to the crank mark and the pink links to the cam marks.

mistakes.title: Reused chain without its paint marks
mistakes.what: Hanging a used chain whose colored links have faded, with no marks added at teardown.
mistakes.consequence: There is no reliable reference and the bank can be a tooth off.
mistakes.prevent: Use the paint marks made at teardown, or fit a new chain.

mistakes.title: Back-face crank mark used
mistakes.what: Lining up the chain to a mark on the back of the crank sprocket.
mistakes.consequence: The crank reference is wrong and the timing is off.
mistakes.prevent: Use the mark on the front face, to the right of the keyway.

mistakes.title: Slack on the guide side
mistakes.what: Hanging the chain with its slack between the sprockets on the fixed guide side.
mistakes.consequence: When the tensioner releases, the slack shifts and the cam moves off its mark.
mistakes.prevent: Keep the chain tight on the guide side and slack on the tensioner side.

steps.title: Install LH tensioner and lever
steps.action: Fit a new O-ring at the LH block half, then the LH tensioner lever and tensioner.

mistakes.title: LH tensioner O-ring missing
mistakes.what: Fitting the LH tensioner without a new O-ring at the block half.
mistakes.consequence: Oil leaks from the feed and the tensioner is starved, letting the chain slap.
mistakes.prevent: Fit a new O-ring at the LH block half every time.

steps.title: Pull the LH stopper pin
steps.action: Recheck the blue and two pink links against their marks, then pull the stopper pin so the tensioner takes up the slack.
steps.why: Once the pin is out the chain is loaded and cannot be shifted a tooth without starting over.

mistakes.title: Tensioner not clicked one notch further
mistakes.what: Pulling the pin without squeezing the chain and guides to let the plunger extend.
mistakes.consequence: The chain is briefly slack and rattles for a moment at start-up.
mistakes.prevent: Squeeze the chain and guides by hand until the plunger clicks one notch further.

mistakes.title: Pin pulled before final mark check
mistakes.what: Releasing the tensioner before rechecking the blue and pink links.
mistakes.consequence: Any tooth error is locked in once the tensioner loads the chain.
mistakes.prevent: Recheck all three marks just before pulling the pin.

mistakes.title: Metal tool levered on a guide
mistakes.what: Pushing on a plastic chain guide with a metal tool for the extra click.
mistakes.consequence: The plastic guide face is gouged and wears quickly against the chain.
mistakes.prevent: Use a plastic screwdriver handle on the guide, never bare metal.

steps.title: Turn over and recheck LH
steps.action: Turn the crank clockwise to confirm nothing binds, then bring it round until the crank and LH marks line up again with the key at six o'clock.
steps.why: The RH chain is timed from this position.

mistakes.title: Turned through a tight spot
mistakes.what: Forcing the crank when it binds during the check.
mistakes.consequence: A valve that is touching a piston is bent by the force.
mistakes.prevent: Stop at any resistance and recheck every mark before going on.
